[state] GARCH-Error OLS Inference Failure State. A market research condition in which OLS t-tests for regression coefficients massively overreject the null hypothesis because errors follow GARCH(1,1) dynamics. With ARCH coefficient alpha=0.35 and GARCH coefficient delta=0.6 (persistence alpha+delta=0.95), empirical rejection rates at the nominal 5% significance level are 15% for T=100 and 33% for T=1000 observations—worsening counterintuitively as sample size grows. The state is active whenever GARCH effects are present in regression residuals and plain OLS inference is applied.
[signature_hamilton_arch_ols_overreject_001] Empirical rejection rate of OLS t-tests substantially exceeding the nominal significance level when regression errors follow GARCH(1,1). With alpha=0.35, delta=0.6 (persistence=0.95), the rejection rate at nominal 5% is 15% for T=100 and 33% for T=1000—a 3x to 7x overrejection factor. The counterintuitive worsening with sample size (T=100 → T=1000) is the key diagnostic observable: under classical asymptotics, larger samples should improve size control, but under persistent ARCH errors the distortion compounds rather than shrinks. Observable by comparing empirical rejection rates in Monte Carlo simulations with known GARCH DGPs against nominal test size. empirical_rejection_rate_at_nominal_5pct; size_distortion_factor; rejection_rate_vs_sample_size_slope; arch_lm_test_statistic Hamilton (ARCH chapter) Figure 2 Monte Carlo evidence. The rejection rate worsening with T is counterintuitive and the key finding: standard asymptotic theory fails under ARCH. The ARCH-LM test on OLS residuals is the practical diagnostic to detect when this failure mode is active.
[claim_hamilton_arch_ols_overreject_001] OLS t-tests for regression coefficients massively overreject the null hypothesis when errors follow GARCH(1,1) with ARCH coefficient alpha=0.35 and GARCH coefficient delta=0.6. The empirical rejection rate at the nominal 5% significance level is 15% for T=100 observations and 33% for T=1000 observations—the distortion worsens as sample size grows. Figure 2, p.8. Monte Carlo simulation results. The worsening with T is especially alarming: conventional asymptotic arguments predict inference improves with sample size, but under ARCH errors the distortion compounds. Parameters alpha=0.35, delta=0.6 imply high persistence (alpha+delta=0.95).
[claim_hamilton_arch_white_ineffective_002] The White (1980) heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard error estimator does not correct OLS inference distortions under ARCH/GARCH errors. HC estimators address cross-sectional heteroscedasticity of unknown form but cannot correct for dynamic conditional heteroscedasticity, where the variance of each error depends on the history of past squared errors. Section 2, p.8-9. White HC is the standard go-to correction for heteroscedasticity in applied econometrics. The failure under ARCH is because ARCH is a serial-correlation property of squared residuals, not a static variance structure.
[policy_hamilton_arch_ols_overreject_001] inference_procedure Before reporting OLS coefficient significance in any financial time-series regression, test residuals for ARCH effects using the ARCH-LM test (Engle 1982) at multiple lags. If ARCH effects are detected, do not use OLS standard errors for inference—switch to GARCH-MLE or bootstrap inference. Include the empirical rejection rate comparison (actual vs. nominal) as a model audit metric in any regression analysis of financial returns. Report p-values with explicit caveats when residuals exhibit GARCH patterns and plain OLS inference was used. Financial econometric models that use OLS regression on return series must include ARCH testing as a mandatory pre-step before inference. When GARCH effects are present, estimation should be performed under the GARCH likelihood (or use GARCH-corrected standard errors) rather than applying plain OLS t-tests. The failure of asymptotic arguments under GARCH (worsening size distortion with larger T) means that large financial datasets do not automatically produce reliable OLS inference—larger T makes the problem worse, not better. The counterintuitive result (distortion worsens with T) is the key policy motivation: practitioners cannot rely on "large sample size = valid inference" when ARCH is present. This applies to all OLS-based factor model estimation, return predictability tests, and risk premium estimation in financial research.
[policy_hamilton_arch_white_ineffective_002] inference_procedure Do not use White (1980) HC standard errors as the correction for ARCH/GARCH effects in financial time-series regressions. When ARCH effects are detected via the ARCH-LM test, White HC is an inappropriate correction; document this explicitly in model validation reports. The appropriate diagnostic sequence: (1) test for ARCH in OLS residuals; (2) if present, re-estimate under GARCH-MLE or use Newey-West HAC standard errors (which address both serial correlation and heteroscedasticity); (3) never substitute White HC as a step-2 action when ARCH is the concern. Model validation pipelines for financial time-series regressions must distinguish the type of heteroscedasticity present: static cross-sectional heteroscedasticity (White HC appropriate) vs. dynamic conditional heteroscedasticity/ARCH (White HC inappropriate). Newey-West HAC standard errors provide a more general correction that accounts for both heteroscedasticity and serial correlation and may be preferred over both White HC and plain OLS as the default for financial time-series inference. This policy implication is a companion to policy_hamilton_arch_ols_overreject_001. The two together define the correct inference approach: (1) detect ARCH, (2) correct with GARCH-MLE or Newey-West HAC, not White HC. References the same OLS inference failure state.
[failure_hamilton_arch_ols_overreject_001] OLS t-tests for regression coefficients produce massively inflated Type I error rates when errors follow GARCH(1,1) with high persistence. At nominal 5% significance, empirical rejection rates reach 15% (T=100) and 33% (T=1000) with alpha=0.35, delta=0.6. The failure worsens as sample size grows—the opposite of what classical asymptotic theory predicts—because ARCH introduces persistent serial correlation in squared errors that OLS standard error formulae cannot accommodate. Financial research using OLS t-tests on returns or factors without ARCH pre-testing will systematically generate spurious rejections, inflating reported statistical significance across the literature. When applying OLS regression with plain t-test inference to financial return series or factor returns that exhibit GARCH effects; when interpreting OLS coefficient significance in time-series regressions without testing for ARCH in residuals; when increasing sample size is expected to improve inference without first addressing the ARCH structure. The counterintuitive worsening with T (15% at T=100 → 33% at T=1000) is the critical distinguishing feature of this failure pattern. In contrast to cross- sectional heteroscedasticity where larger T helps, GARCH errors create a compounding problem. False positive risk is very high: with T=1000 observations and a nominal 5% test, 33% of true null hypotheses are rejected—nearly 7x overrejection.
[failure_hamilton_arch_white_ineffective_002] The White (1980) heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard error estimator does not correct OLS inference distortions when regression errors follow ARCH/GARCH dynamics. [state] GARCH Volatility Clustering Persistence State. A market condition characterized by persistent clustering of return volatility— large shocks followed by further large shocks and small shocks followed by further small shocks—captured by a GARCH(1,1) conditional variance process h_t = omega + alpha * u_{t-1}^2 + delta * h_{t-1}. High persistence (alpha + delta near 1, delta close to 1) implies slow mean-reversion of conditional variance following a shock, producing extended periods of elevated or depressed volatility. The state is active whenever GARCH persistence parameters are large and squared-return autocorrelations are significant.

Measured by the Ljung-Box Q-statistic on squared residuals and the autocorrelation function (ACF) of squared returns. In GARCH(1,1) terms, high persistence (delta close to 1, alpha+delta near 1) produces slow mean-reversion of conditional variance after shocks. Observable as extended runs of high-volatility or low-volatility trading days in any major financial return series. squared_return_autocorrelation; absolute_return_autocorrelation; ljung_box_q_stat_squared_residuals; garch_persistence_parameter_sum Foundational observable motivating GARCH modeling. The ACF of squared returns (not raw returns) is the primary diagnostic; raw returns are approximately uncorrelated while squared returns exhibit significant autocorrelation. This distinguishes GARCH effects from mean autocorrelation.
[claim_hamilton_arch_volatility_clustering_004] GARCH(1,1) captures the empirical stylized fact of volatility clustering— large shocks followed by large shocks and small shocks followed by small shocks—through the GARCH persistence parameter delta. Values near 1 indicate near-IGARCH behavior (near-permanent volatility shocks); values well below 1 indicate faster mean-reversion. This foundational stylized fact is well-established; the policy implication is a reminder that GARCH is the required default for financial time series, not an optional enhancement. [state] Real-Time Filtered Regime Probability State. A market condition description defined by the real-time probability that each discrete Markov regime is active, computed recursively by the Hamilton (1989) filter. At each time t, the filter yields xi_{jt} = Pr(s_t=j | Omega_t) via a two-step prediction-update recursion: (1) prediction xi_{t|t-1} = A^T * xi_{t-1|t-1} using the transition matrix A; (2) update xi_{t|t} proportional to the elementwise product of the conditional density vector f(y_t | s_t, Omega_{t-1}) and xi_{t|t-1}. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood via this filter. The state is active whenever a Markov regime-switching model is estimated and real-time regime inference is required.
[signature_hamilton_rs_filter_equations_001] The Hamilton filter produces a time series of real-time filtered regime probabilities xi_{jt} = Pr(s_t=j | Omega_t) for each regime j at each time t. Observable outputs: (1) filtered probabilities xi_{t|t} (real-time, using only information up to t); (2) smoothed probabilities xi_{t|T} from the Kim backward smoother (full-sample); (3) the log-likelihood of the data under the model; (4) one-step-ahead forecast densities f(y_{t+1} | Omega_t). The filtered probability time series provides a continuous-valued indicator of current regime activation. Sharp transitions in xi_{jt} identify regime change-points; persistent high values indicate prolonged regime occupancy. filtered_regime_probability_time_series; smoothed_regime_probability_time_series; log_likelihood_value; one_step_ahead_forecast_density; regime_change_point_dates The Hamilton filter output is the primary instrument for real-time regime monitoring. Filtered (not smoothed) probabilities are the operational signal for real-time allocation decisions; smoothed probabilities are appropriate for retrospective analysis only.

A regime-modeling condition in which combining Markov regime switching with GARCH conditional variance makes the variance at time t depend on the full past regime path. [claim_hamilton_rs_garch_extensions_003] Regime-switching GARCH (RS-GARCH) models face a path-dependence problem: the conditional variance at time t depends on all past regime states, making likelihood evaluation computationally intractable as the state history grows exponentially. Gray (1996) and Haas, Mittnik, and Paolella (2004) propose tractable approximations by collapsing the state history at each step. p.1-9. The path-dependence problem is a key practical limitation of combining Markov regime-switching with GARCH volatility dynamics. Without an approximation, the number of terms in the likelihood grows as 2^T for a two-state model.
[policy_hamilton_rs_garch_extensions_003] model_specification When combining regime-switching with within-regime GARCH volatility dynamics, require that the implementation uses a tractable path-collapsing approximation (Gray 1996 or Haas-Mittnik-Paolella 2004 approach) rather than naive exact RS-GARCH. Include the approximation method and its reference in model documentation. Validate that the RS-GARCH implementation produces a finite log-likelihood and converges under MLE before using the model in production. Flag any RS-GARCH implementation that attempts exact path enumeration as computationally infeasible. Do not implement RS-GARCH from scratch without applying the state-collapsing approximation that makes the likelihood tractable. Use established implementations (e.g., MSwM, MSGARCH packages in R; or custom Python implementations following Gray 1996 / HMP 2004) that already incorporate tractable approximations. When model complexity or latency constraints are tight, consider using regime-switching with constant within-regime variance (no GARCH component) as a simpler and fully tractable alternative. The path-dependence problem grows exponentially with the number of states (K^T for K states). For two states, even T=50 observations yields 2^50 ≈ 10^15 paths— computationally infeasible. The Gray 1996 and HMP 2004 approximations reduce this to O(T * K^2) computation by collapsing the state distribution at each step.
[failure_hamilton_rs_garch_extensions_003] Naive RS-GARCH model implementation is computationally intractable due to exponential path-dependence. The conditional variance at time t in an RS-GARCH model depends on all past regime realizations s_1, ..., s_{t-1}, causing the number of distinct variance paths to grow as 2^T for a two-state model. Direct likelihood evaluation requires summing over all 2^T paths, making exact inference infeasible for any practical sample size. Models that attempt to combine regime-switching and GARCH without applying tractable approximations (e.g., Gray 1996; Haas, Mittnik, and Paolella 2004 state-collapsing methods) will fail to produce likelihood values and cannot be estimated via standard MLE. When attempting to combine Markov regime-switching with within-regime GARCH volatility dynamics without applying a tractable path-collapsing approximation; when implementing RS-GARCH naively using standard Markov-switching software that does not account for the path-dependence problem; when the number of states K and sample size T are large enough to make 2^T path enumeration computationally infeasible (practically, T > 20 already causes intractability). Gray (1996) and Haas et al. (2004) provide the standard tractable approximations by collapsing regime history at each time step rather than tracking all 2^T paths. False negative risk is high: practitioners implementing RS-GARCH without awareness of path-dependence may encounter numerical failures that appear to be optimization problems rather than fundamental model design issues.

Flag any RS-GARCH implementation that attempts exact path enumeration as computationally infeasible. Do not implement RS-GARCH from scratch without applying the state-collapsing approximation that makes the likelihood tractable. Use established implementations (e.g., MSwM, MSGARCH packages in R; or custom Python implementations following Gray 1996 / HMP 2004) that already incorporate tractable approximations. When model complexity or latency constraints are tight, consider using regime-switching with constant within-regime variance (no GARCH component) as a simpler and fully tractable alternative. The path-dependence problem grows exponentially with the number of states (K^T for K states). For two states, even T=50 observations yields 2^50 ≈ 10^15 paths— computationally infeasible. The Gray 1996 and HMP 2004 approximations reduce this to O(T * K^2) computation by collapsing the state distribution at each step.

Naive RS-GARCH model implementation is computationally intractable due to exponential path-dependence. The conditional variance at time t in an RS-GARCH model depends on all past regime realizations s_1, ..., s_{t-1}, causing the number of distinct variance paths to grow as 2^T for a two-state model. Direct likelihood evaluation requires summing over all 2^T paths, making exact inference infeasible for any practical sample size. Models that attempt to combine regime-switching and GARCH without applying tractable approximations (e.g., Gray 1996; Haas, Mittnik, and Paolella 2004 state-collapsing methods) will fail to produce likelihood values and cannot be estimated via standard MLE. When attempting to combine Markov regime-switching with within-regime GARCH volatility dynamics without applying a tractable path-collapsing approximation; when implementing RS-GARCH naively using standard Markov-switching software that does not account for the path-dependence problem; when the number of states K and sample size T are large enough to make 2^T path enumeration computationally infeasible (practically, T > 20 already causes intractability). Gray (1996) and Haas et al. (2004) provide the standard tractable approximations by collapsing regime history at each time step rather than tracking all 2^T paths. False negative risk is high: practitioners implementing RS-GARCH without awareness of path-dependence may encounter numerical failures that appear to be optimization problems rather than fundamental model design issues.

[state] January-Concentrated Illiquidity Premium Seasonal Regime. A seasonal market state in which the cross-sectional relationship between effective trading costs and future stock returns is concentrated in January. Outside of January, the illiquidity premium is substantially weaker or absent. The January concentration is consistent with year-end tax-loss selling and January rebalancing effects, and with the disproportionate illiquidity of small-cap stocks subject to the January effect. Documented over the 1926-2006 CRSP NYSE/AMEX sample.
[signature_hasbrouck_january_effect_004] Calendar month = January as the conditioning signal for the illiquidity return premium. The return-cost relationship is substantially stronger in January than in other calendar months; outside January the premium is substantially weaker or absent. The observable indicator is the calendar month flag combined with cross-sectional Gibbs effective cost decile rank, with January identified as the active-premium month. calendar_month; gibbs_effective_cost_decile_rank; monthly_return_by_cost_decile_january_vs_non_january January is the month-of-year indicator that activates the illiquidity premium signal. Non-January months should be treated as a different return regime for liquidity-based cross-sectional predictions.
[claim_hasbrouck_january_effect_004] The cross-sectional relationship between effective trading costs and stock returns is concentrated in January. Outside of January, the illiquidity premium in the 1926-2006 sample is substantially weaker or absent, suggesting the return-liquidity relationship is driven primarily by year-end tax-loss selling and January rebalancing effects. Section I.D, p.1445-1453. Seasonal decomposition of the illiquidity return premium. The January concentration is consistent with the broader small-stock January effect literature and the disproportionate illiquidity of small-cap stocks.
[policy_hasbrouck_january_effect_004] activity_suppression Condition the illiquidity return premium feature on calendar month. In January, the illiquidity premium feature may be included at full weight. Outside of January (February through December), reduce or suppress the illiquidity premium feature weight, as the cross-sectional return-cost relationship is substantially weaker or absent. Cross-sectional return models should incorporate a January indicator variable when using effective cost as a predictor. A model that applies the illiquidity premium uniformly across calendar months will overstate its year-round contribution. Confidence in the illiquidity premium predictor is high in January; substantially lower outside January based on 1926-2006 CRSP evidence. Suppress or heavily downweight the illiquidity premium cross-sectional feature in non-January months (February through December) for CRSP NYSE/AMEX equities. The January concentration likely reflects small-stock tax-loss selling and year-end rebalancing. Policy applies to the cross-sectional illiquidity premium only; time-series liquidity measures are not necessarily affected by this seasonal pattern.
[failure_hasbrouck_january_effect_004] The cross-sectional illiquidity return premium is substantially weaker or absent outside of January. A model or feature relying on the return-cost relationship as a persistent monthly predictor will produce unreliable signals in non-January months (February through December), because the premium documented over 1926-2006 is concentrated in January. Using the illiquidity premium signal without calendar-month conditioning overstates its year-round predictive power. Active outside calendar month January. The illiquidity premium feature is unreliable (substantially weaker or absent) in February through December for CRSP NYSE/AMEX equities. The January concentration likely reflects the small-stock January effect and year-end tax-loss selling. The failure mode is not estimator error but a structural limitation of the premium itself outside its seasonal window.

[state] Gibbs Estimator Small-Sample Bias Regime. A microstructure estimation state in which a stock-month observation window contains too few daily transactions for the Gibbs sampler to reliably observe spread-induced serial price reversals. In this regime, the estimator underestimates or produces unreliable effective cost estimates because the probability of detecting the signature price-reversal pattern is low with sparse data. Disproportionately affects small-cap and illiquid stocks.
[claim_hasbrouck_small_sample_bias_005] Monthly Gibbs effective cost estimates are biased when the number of transactions within a month is small. With few daily observations, the likelihood of observing spread-induced serial price reversals is low, causing the Gibbs sampler to underestimate or unreliably estimate c. The estimator performs reliably only when monthly trade counts are sufficiently large. Section I.C, p.1445-1453. Practical limitation of the Gibbs approach. Affects small-cap and illiquid stocks disproportionately. In practice, a minimum monthly observation count is recommended before trusting the Gibbs estimate for a given stock-month.
[policy_hasbrouck_small_sample_bias_005] confidence_calibration Apply a data quality filter to Gibbs effective cost features: exclude or flag stock-months below a minimum monthly observation threshold. This is especially important for small-cap and illiquid stocks and for early historical periods with sparser daily coverage. Require a minimum monthly transaction (daily observation) count before trusting the Gibbs effective cost estimate for a given stock-month. Stock-months with insufficient observation counts should have their Gibbs estimates excluded or heavily discounted. Do not use Gibbs estimates for small-cap and illiquid stocks in sparse observation periods without filtering on minimum monthly count. Suppress Gibbs effective cost features for stock-months where monthly transaction (daily observation) count is below the practitioner-determined reliability threshold. The source does not quantify the exact minimum count threshold; practitioners must determine an appropriate cutoff. The bias direction is underestimation of c, which would understate true illiquidity and underweight genuinely illiquid stocks.
[failure_hasbrouck_small_sample_bias_005] The Gibbs sampler effective cost estimator produces biased or unreliable estimates of c when the number of daily transactions within a month is small. With few observations, the probability of detecting spread-induced serial price reversals is low, causing the estimator to underestimate or unreliably estimate the effective cost. The failure disproportionately affects small-cap and illiquid stocks, which tend to have fewer monthly transactions, and worsens in historical periods with sparser data coverage. Monthly transaction (daily observation) count for a given stock-month falls below a reliable estimation threshold. Exact threshold is not quantified in the source but a minimum monthly count is required. Affects primarily small-cap and illiquid stocks. This is a practical data-sparsity limitation of the Gibbs/Roll estimator, not a theoretical defect. The estimator performs well when monthly observation counts are sufficient. Practitioners should filter out stock-months below a minimum count threshold.

[state] Multi-Asset Time-Series Momentum Trend Following State. A market condition in which time-series momentum (TSMOM) signals deliver persistent risk-adjusted excess returns across diversified multi-asset futures portfolios. Characterized by: (1) individual-asset Sharpe ratios that increase monotonically with signal look-back horizon—0.29 (1-month), 0.36 (3-month), 0.38 (12-month)—averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts; (2) a diversified 58-instrument TSMOM portfolio achieving ~1.8 gross annualized Sharpe at 10% vol target (January 1985–June 2012); (3) a "smile" return pattern—best performance in sustained trending environments (strong bull or bear markets), worst in trendless choppy markets—with near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02); (4) after controlling for a simple diversified TSMOM factor, all managed futures fund net-of-fee alphas become negative under 2-and-20 fee structures (~6% average annual fee drag). Most CTAs exhibit dominant exposure to the 3-month TSMOM signal rather than the individually optimal 12-month horizon, and systematically overweight fixed income. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010), evidence_tier 2 (practitioner paper with direct empirical content).
[signature_hurst_mf_cta_factor_loading_005] Observable pattern in managed futures fund TSMOM factor loadings revealing systematic underexposure to the individually optimal long-horizon (12-month) signal and overexposure to the suboptimal 3-month signal. The signature is detectable as: (1) regression of CTA fund net returns on the 1m, 3m, and 12m TSMOM factors shows the 3-month factor carrying the highest average loading across funds, despite the 12-month signal having the highest individual- asset Sharpe (0.38 vs. 0.36 and 0.29); (2) R-squared of 0.36–0.64 for individual fund returns on the diversified TSMOM factor, confirming that systematic trend following explains the majority of return variation while leaving unexplained residual variation potentially attributable to asset class tilts; (3) elevated fixed income factor loading relative to an equal- volatility multi-asset benchmark—indicating systematic overweight of bond futures relative to the theoretical optimum; (4) net-of-fee alpha becoming negative for all funds after TSMOM factor control, confirming that the loading pattern explains essentially all of net return. Estimated from CTA fund database regression analysis, approximately 1985–2012. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010). cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_1m; cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_3m; cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_12m; cta_fund_r_squared_vs_tsmom; cta_fund_fixed_income_weight; cta_fund_net_alpha_post_tsmom The 3-month dominant loading across CTAs may reflect rational adaptation to operational constraints (AUM-driven capacity limits at shorter horizons force migration away from the shortest signals; client preference for lower volatility implementations may favor medium-length horizons). The fixed income overweight reflects the dominant bond bull market of 1985–2012 which benefited any fund with above-benchmark bond exposure. The loading pattern provides a diagnostic for identifying horizon-biased managed futures programs relative to the empirically optimal 12-month dominant allocation.
[signature_hurst_tsmom_horizon_sharpe_001] Observable monotone gradient of individual-asset Sharpe ratios with time-series momentum look-back horizon, combined with a large diversification benefit in a multi-asset portfolio. The signature is detectable as: (1) individual-asset TSMOM Sharpe ratios increasing from 0.29 (1-month horizon) to 0.36 (3-month) to 0.38 (12-month), averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts (commodities, equities, bonds, currencies), confirming that longer look-back windows capture more persistent trend signals; (2) the diversified portfolio Sharpe (~1.8 gross at 10% vol target) substantially exceeding the individual-asset average (0.38), demonstrating large cross-asset diversification benefit; (3) the portfolio achieves approximately 18% gross annualized return at 10% vol. Computed over January 1985–June 2012. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010). tsmom_1m_sharpe_individual; tsmom_3m_sharpe_individual; tsmom_12m_sharpe_individual; diversified_portfolio_sharpe; annualized_volatility_target; cross_asset_diversification_ratio The horizon-Sharpe gradient (0.29 / 0.36 / 0.38) is computed at the individual instrument level. The diversified portfolio at 12-month horizon achieves ~1.8 gross Sharpe, implying a diversification gain of approximately 4.7x relative to the individual-asset average (0.38). All figures are gross of fees and transaction costs; net returns are materially lower under 2-and-20 fee structures (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003).
[signature_hurst_tsmom_smile_004] Conditional return profile of time-series momentum strategies exhibiting a "smile" shape with respect to market regime, confirming trend-following diversification value. The signature is observable as: (1) highest TSMOM returns during sustained directional equity market environments (both strong bull and strong bear markets, corresponding to the tails of the trailing equity return distribution); (2) lowest or negative TSMOM returns during trendless, high-volatility choppy markets; (3) near-zero unconditional correlation with S&P 500 (~-0.02 over January 1985–June 2012). The smile pattern reflects the strategy design: TSMOM profits most when assets trend consistently in one direction over the formation period, which occurs most reliably during sustained directional moves. The near-zero equity correlation confirms that TSMOM is not a directional equity bet but a conditional diversifier. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010) Figure 2. tsmom_returns_by_equity_market_decile; sp500_correlation_unconditional; trailing_equity_return; tsmom_conditional_sharpe The smile pattern is consistent with the Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012) finding of best TSMOM performance in extreme market months. The near-zero equity correlation (~-0.02) combined with the smile pattern makes TSMOM a particularly valuable crisis hedge: it tends to perform best precisely when equity portfolios suffer most, although this is a conditional (not guaranteed) property. Identification requires decile-conditional return analysis, not just an unconditional correlation.
[claim_hurst_mf_alpha_after_tsmom_003] After controlling for a simple diversified time-series momentum factor, the net-of-fee alpha of every managed futures fund in the sample becomes negative. A 2-and-20 fee structure (2% management fee, 20% performance fee) applied to the diversified TSMOM strategy implies an average annual fee load of approximately 6% on the gross return, which exceeds the alpha individual managers generate beyond the systematic trend signal. Section IV of Hurst et al. (2013) regresses individual managed futures fund net returns on the diversified TSMOM factor. Pre-fee, funds show positive but modest alpha; post-fee, all funds show negative alpha. The paper estimates the fee load by simulating 2-and-20 on the TSMOM gross return series, finding ~6% average annual fee drag. High R-squared values (0.36–0.64) confirm that TSMOM explains most managed futures return variation.
[claim_hurst_mf_diversified_sharpe_002] A diversified time-series momentum strategy across 58 liquid futures contracts achieves a gross annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 1.8 at a 10% annualized volatility target, over the period January 1985 through June 2012. This represents a substantial diversification benefit over the individual asset average Sharpe of 0.38 (12-month horizon). Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013) Table 2 and Section III report the diversified TSMOM portfolio performance. The portfolio volatility-scales each of the 58 positions to a common ex-ante 10% annual volatility, then combines them equally. The resulting Sharpe of ~1.8 (gross) reflects cross-asset diversification. The paper uses this as the benchmark replication of managed futures industry returns.
[claim_hurst_mf_horizon_sharpe_001] For individual assets, the Sharpe ratio of a time-series momentum strategy increases monotonically with the signal look-back horizon across the 1-month, 3-month, and 12-month horizons: 0.29, 0.36, and 0.38 respectively, averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts. Longer look-back horizons consistently outperform shorter look-back horizons at the individual asset level. Table 1 of Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013 JOIM / 2010 working paper) reports individual-instrument Sharpe ratios for TSMOM strategies with formation periods of 1 month, 3 months, and 12 months. Averages across all 58 instruments show the monotone horizon pattern. Authors note the 12-month signal dominates in the individual asset setting but that diversification benefits are largest at shorter horizons.
[claim_hurst_mf_manager_horizon_bias_005] Most managed futures managers in the sample weight medium- to long-term trend signals (3-month horizon dominant) and systematically overweight fixed income relative to the equal-volatility benchmark. The typical manager's signal mix more closely resembles a 3-month TSMOM factor than a 12-month one, despite the 12-month signal having the highest individual-asset Sharpe ratio. Section IV.B of Hurst et al. (2013) decomposes the exposures of individual managed futures funds to TSMOM factors at 1m, 3m, and 12m horizons. The factor loading analysis shows that the 3-month TSMOM factor has the highest average loading across funds, suggesting most CTAs operate in the medium-term trend space. Asset class analysis shows above-benchmark fixed income weights (bonds and rates) in the typical fund.
[claim_hurst_mf_smile_pattern_004] Time-series momentum exhibits a "smile" return pattern: it performs best during prolonged bear or bull market environments and worst during trendless, choppy markets. Over the full 1985–2012 sample, TSMOM has near-zero correlation with the S&P 500 (approximately -0.02), confirming that the strategy is not a directional equity bet. Figure 2 and Section III.B of Hurst et al. (2013) analyze TSMOM returns conditional on trailing equity market returns and market volatility. The smile pattern emerges from the strategy's design: TSMOM profits most when assets trend consistently in one direction over the formation period, which occurs most reliably during sustained bull or bear markets. The near-zero S&P correlation is calculated from the full monthly return series.
[policy_hurst_mf_diversification_risk_control_002] risk_control The ~4.7x diversification benefit (individual-asset Sharpe 0.38 → diversified portfolio Sharpe 1.8 gross) documented by Hurst et al. (2013) implies that concentration in a subset of the 58-instrument universe materially degrades risk-adjusted returns. Risk control features: (1) instrument-count tracker— reducing the active instrument count below ~40 of the 58-instrument benchmark will erode a disproportionate share of the diversification premium; (2) asset class coverage indicator—equal representation across the four asset classes (commodities, equities, bonds, currencies) is required to capture the full diversification benefit; missing asset classes should trigger risk alerts; (3) volatility concentration metric—verify that no single instrument or asset class accounts for more than 30–35% of total portfolio volatility, consistent with a well-diversified 10%-vol-target-per-instrument construction; (4) S&P 500 correlation monitor—near-zero unconditional correlation (~-0.02) is the risk neutrality benchmark; positive correlation spikes signal unintended equity factor loading. Model the diversified TSMOM benchmark gross Sharpe (~1.8) as the target achievable only with a full multi-asset futures universe (58+ liquid instruments). Concentrated implementations (e.g., equities-only or commodities-only TSMOM) should be expected to produce Sharpe ratios substantially below 1.8, closer to the individual-asset average of 0.38. Risk controls should enforce minimum asset-class breadth requirements and track the diversification ratio as a forward-looking Sharpe degradation indicator when instruments are dropped from the universe. Confidence in achieving gross Sharpe near 1.8 requires: (1) all four asset classes represented with approximately equal volatility contribution; (2) active instrument count above 40; (3) near-zero S&P 500 correlation. Deviations from any of these conditions should trigger proportional reductions in expected Sharpe from the 1.8 benchmark. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe at 10% vol target is a full-universe, equal-volatility- weighted benchmark. It is gross of fees; after typical 2-and-20 managed futures fee structures, net Sharpe is substantially lower (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003). The 10%-per-instrument volatility target methodology normalizes position sizes across diverse asset classes; deviations from this normalization will produce concentration that degrades the diversification benefit.
[policy_hurst_mf_fee_structure_calibration_003] confidence_calibration Confidence calibration for managed futures fund returns must account for the ~6% average annual fee drag under 2-and-20 structures, as documented by Hurst et al. (2013). The fee calibration features are: (1) fund-level fee structure identifier—management fee percentage plus performance fee percentage; (2) gross-to-net return conversion applying the documented 2% management fee plus 20% performance fee to the TSMOM gross return series; (3) TSMOM R-squared for each fund return series (0.36–0.64 range documented)—funds with higher R-squared are more TSMOM-driven and thus more susceptible to complete fee erosion of systematic alpha; (4) post-fee alpha relative to the TSMOM factor— the primary evidence metric, which is negative for all documented funds under 2-and-20 after TSMOM factor control. When classifying managed futures fund returns as evidence for the trend-following state, apply a fee-adjusted confidence weighting: gross TSMOM performance (~1.8 Sharpe) is strong evidence for the underlying trend-following state, but managed futures fund net performance is not an independent confirmation. After controlling for the TSMOM factor and deducting ~6% annual fee load, fund net alpha is negative—indicating no incremental information about trend-following state strength beyond what the systematic TSMOM factor already captures. Confidence in the underlying trend-following state should be calibrated to the gross systematic TSMOM factor performance, not to managed fund net returns. Do not use managed futures fund net-of-fee returns as confirmation of the trend-following state's activity. Use the diversified TSMOM factor gross return (targeting ~1.8 Sharpe at 10% vol) as the state indicator. Managed fund net returns understate state strength due to fee extraction; gross factor performance overstates achievable net investor return. Calibrate investor-accessible expected return at the lower-fee implementation level (e.g., systematic rules-based fund with ~0.5–1% expense ratio rather than 2-and-20). The 6% average annual fee load estimate is approximate and derived by simulating 2% management plus 20% performance fee on the TSMOM gross return series (Hurst et al., Section IV). Actual fee loads vary by fund and period; the documented range of R-squared (0.36–0.64) means funds with higher TSMOM beta will have proportionally higher systematic fee drag. The policy conclusion (use systematic low-cost TSMOM exposure rather than managed fund vehicles to access the trend premium) follows directly from the fee analysis but is a policy interpretation, not a direct stated conclusion of the paper.
[policy_hurst_mf_regime_conditional_activity_004] activity_suppression The smile pattern of TSMOM returns documented by Hurst et al. (2013)—best performance during sustained bull and bear markets, worst during trendless choppy markets—implies that activity should be conditioned on the current equity market regime. Features for regime-conditional TSMOM activity: (1) trailing equity market return over 3–12 months as a regime indicator— directional markets (strong positive or strong negative trailing returns) correspond to the "smile tails" where TSMOM performs best; (2) equity market volatility regime indicator—high volatility combined with low directional trend (choppy regime) signals the worst environment for TSMOM; (3) conditional return decile rank of trailing equity return—TSMOM performs best in the top and bottom deciles, worst in the middle deciles; (4) S&P 500 unconditional correlation monitor (~-0.02 target)—a significant positive deviation signals unintended directional equity exposure that may distort the smile pattern. Do not assume TSMOM delivers uniform returns across market regimes. Condition model confidence and signal weighting on the current equity market regime: increase TSMOM signal weight during sustained directional regimes (top or bottom decile of trailing equity returns) and reduce weight during choppy indeterminate regimes. The 1.8 gross Sharpe is an unconditional average; regime-conditional expected Sharpe varies substantially above and below this level. Near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02) is the target; sustained positive correlation indicates the portfolio has drifted from its diversifying character. Confidence in TSMOM state returns is highest in sustained directional market environments (both bull and bear, consistent with the smile tails). Reduce confidence in trendless or high-volatility choppy regimes where TSMOM historically shows near-zero or negative returns. Activity suppression is warranted in confirmed choppy regimes where trailing equity return occupies the middle deciles for 3+ consecutive months. Suppress full TSMOM activity allocation when the trailing equity market return occupies middle deciles (approximately 4th through 7th deciles) for sustained periods (3+ months), signaling a trendless choppy regime inconsistent with the smile pattern's optimal conditions. Maintain reduced-activity (not zero) allocation to preserve exposure for the transition back to a sustained directional regime, as the smile pattern requires maintained positioning to benefit from sudden trend emergence. The smile pattern is a conditional average, not a regime classifier with a sharp entry/exit threshold. The practical implication is proportional weighting adjustment rather than binary on/off switching. The near-zero S&P 500 unconditional correlation (~-0.02) applies over the full 1985–2012 sample; within the smile pattern, TSMOM is positively correlated to equities during bull markets (both moving in the same direction) and negatively correlated during bear markets (where TSMOM profits from short positions).
[policy_hurst_tsmom_diversified_001] model_weighting When the multi-asset trend following state is classified as active, emphasize: (1) diversified TSMOM signals across all available asset classes (commodities, equities, fixed income, currencies) to capture the ~4.7x diversification benefit relative to individual-asset Sharpe; (2) volatility-scaled position sizing per instrument (target 10% annualized vol per instrument before combination, consistent with the Hurst et al. benchmark methodology); (3) smile-pattern conditioning: weight TSMOM signals more heavily when trailing equity market returns indicate a sustained directional regime (both bull and bear tails), and reduce weight in trendless high-volatility environments. De-emphasize TSMOM signals when the market is in a mean- reverting choppy regime incompatible with sustained directional moves. The gross diversified TSMOM Sharpe of ~1.8 (January 1985–June 2012) is the benchmark for a fully diversified implementation with proper volatility scaling. Models should not use individual-asset Sharpe ratios (0.29–0.38) as the expected portfolio Sharpe; the diversification benefit is essential. After applying 2-and-20 fee structures, the net-of-fee alpha becomes negative (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003); a low-cost systematic implementation (e.g., factor-based) is required to capture meaningful net investor return. Highest confidence in the TSMOM state when: the equity market is in a sustained directional regime (consistent with the smile pattern); the portfolio is diversified across all four asset classes with proper vol-scaling; and implementation costs are below the 6% annual fee-load threshold that eliminates net alpha. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe is computed over January 1985–June 2012 (a 27-year sample dominated by a secular bond bull market and multiple sustained equity bear and bull markets). The volatility target normalization (10% per instrument) is central to achieving the diversification benefit; without it, single-asset concentration dominates. Near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02) is the key portfolio construction argument for institutional allocation.
[policy_hurst_tsmom_horizon_selection_001] feature_selection Horizon selection for TSMOM signals should be governed by individual-asset Sharpe evidence (12-month dominant at 0.38) rather than by observed manager allocations (3-month dominant in CTA databases). The typical CTA horizon bias toward 3-month signals reflects capacity constraints and operational factors, not a superior signal horizon at moderate AUM. Policy for feature construction: (1) weight the 12-month look-back most heavily in the signal composite for strategies operating below institutional capacity limits; (2) include shorter-horizon signals (1-month, 3-month) for diversification within the momentum-horizon space; (3) monitor whether capacity pressure forces migration toward shorter horizons (reducing individual-asset Sharpe from 0.38 toward 0.29) as AUM scales; (4) avoid systematic fixed income overweight inherited from typical CTA factor exposures during the secular bond bull market period. Model the multi-asset TSMOM state with horizon-weighted signal construction favoring 12-month signals at the individual-asset level (Sharpe 0.38 vs. 0.29 and 0.36 for 1m and 3m). At the portfolio level, the diversification benefit largely equalizes horizon differences; the primary horizon choice matters most for individual-instrument signal quality. Separately model the manager-allocation landscape (typically 3-month dominant) versus the empirically optimal allocation (12-month dominant) to correctly attribute observed CTA returns to the factor mix. When CTA fund exposures are predominantly 3-month-horizon, expect gross Sharpe below the theoretically achievable 0.38 individual-asset benchmark. Confidence in maximum-Sharpe signal construction requires empirical confirmation that 12-month dominance has not been arbitraged away in the post-2012 period. The policy recommendation to emphasize 12-month signals applies specifically to the empirical context of Hurst et al. (2013) using 58 liquid futures contracts over 1985–2012. Post-2012 evidence should be used to recalibrate the optimal horizon given potential changes in market efficiency. The fixed income overweight in typical CTAs was beneficial during the secular bond bull market; this tailwind may not persist under rising rate environments.
[failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003] The trend-following momentum state delivers robust gross returns but fails to generate positive net-of-fee alpha for investors in managed futures funds under standard 2-and-20 fee structures. After controlling for a simple diversified time-series momentum factor, every managed futures fund in the Hurst et al. (2013) sample shows negative net-of-fee alpha; the average annual fee drag under a 2% management fee plus 20% performance fee applied to the TSMOM gross return series is approximately 6% per year. High R-squared values of 0.36–0.64 confirm that the TSMOM factor explains the majority of managed futures return variation, leaving little room for manager skill-based alpha net of costs. A model that uses gross TSMOM Sharpe ratios (~1.8) without fee adjustment overestimates net investor return by approximately 6 percentage points per year, confusing the availability of the underlying trend premium with the value-add of managed fund vehicles as delivery mechanisms for that premium. When managed futures fund gross returns are used without deducting the ~6% average annual fee load under 2-and-20 structures; when manager selection is premised on gross alpha rather than post-fee alpha; when the TSMOM systematic factor is not controlled for in performance attribution; when the R-squared of fund returns on the TSMOM factor (0.36–0.64) is not accounted for in skill-based interpretation. The finding that all funds show negative net-of-fee alpha does not mean trend following is unprofitable; it means that the fee structure transfers the majority of the systematic trend premium from investors to managers. A lower-fee vehicle (e.g., a systematic rules-based trend ETF with ~0.5% expense ratio) capturing the same TSMOM exposure would preserve most of the gross ~1.8 Sharpe benefit for end investors. The 6% average fee load is approximate and varies with the specific gross return realization in each period.
[failure_hurst_mf_horizon_bias_005] Managed futures managers systematically underexpose their portfolios to the individually optimal 12-month look-back horizon signal, operating predominantly at the 3-month horizon, and overweight fixed income relative to a balanced equal-volatility multi-asset benchmark. Factor loading analysis of CTA fund returns against 1m, 3m, and 12m TSMOM factors shows the 3-month factor carries the highest average loading across funds, despite the 12-month signal achieving the highest individual-asset Sharpe (0.38 vs 0.29 and 0.36). The systematic underweighting of the 12-month signal means managers collectively leave Sharpe ratio on the table relative to the empirical optimum. Additionally, the fixed income overweight (above equal-volatility benchmark levels) exposes the typical CTA portfolio to a secular bond market tailwind during the 1985–2012 sample period that may not persist. A model treating managed futures fund exposures as representative of the optimal TSMOM signal mix will misclassify the active horizon allocation as evidence that 3-month is the superior horizon, when it instead reflects behavioral and operational biases. When CTA fund factor loadings are used to infer the optimal TSMOM signal horizon mix rather than the horizon that maximizes Sharpe; when the fixed income overweight in typical CTA portfolios is not adjusted for secular bond bull market tailwinds during the estimation period (1985–2012); when manager horizon selection is interpreted as reflecting signal quality rather than capacity constraints, AUM-driven turnover limits, or client preferences for lower volatility (shorter-horizon signals have lower individual Sharpes but may have lower tail risk in certain regimes). The medium-term (3-month) dominance in CTA exposures may reflect rational capacity management: longer-horizon signals require larger position sizes in given instruments and are harder to scale without market impact at large AUM. Shorter-horizon signals offer higher turnover but lower capacity. The optimal horizon in practice depends on AUM, instrument liquidity, and execution costs—factors not captured by the gross Sharpe comparison.
[failure_hurst_mf_short_horizon_underperformance_001] Portfolios constructed with a dominant 1-month TSMOM signal (individual-asset Sharpe 0.29) systematically underperform those using a 12-month dominant signal (Sharpe 0.38), leaving approximately 0.09 Sharpe ratio units on the table at the individual-asset level before diversification. The monotone gradient from Hurst et al. (2013)—SR 0.29 (1m), 0.36 (3m), 0.38 (12m) averaged across 58 liquid futures—implies that every unit of signal weight shifted from longer to shorter horizons at the individual-instrument level degrades expected gross Sharpe in proportion to that weight shift. A model that assigns equal horizon weights (1/3 to each of 1m, 3m, 12m) without adjusting for the empirical gradient will underestimate achievable Sharpe by approximately 0.04–0.05 units relative to the 12m-dominant weighted optimum. This failure is distinct from the manager horizon bias failure (failure_hurst_mf_horizon_bias_005): here, the failure is in model design (choosing a suboptimal horizon weighting scheme), not in practitioner behavior. The failure is most consequential at moderate AUM where capacity constraints do not yet force migration to shorter horizons. When TSMOM signal construction assigns equal or higher weight to 1-month or 3-month horizons than to the 12-month horizon without capacity-driven justification; when the horizon-Sharpe gradient (0.29/0.36/0.38) is not used to inform signal weighting; when shorter-horizon signals are added for diversification benefit without confirming that the diversification gain outweighs the individual-asset Sharpe reduction; when the dominant CTA horizon allocation (3-month heavy, as documented by Hurst et al.) is adopted as the default without checking whether the operational justifications (AUM capacity, client expectations) apply to the modeled strategy. The failure is most clearly expressed at the individual-asset level (SR 0.29 vs 0.38 over the 58-instrument average). At the diversified portfolio level, combining all three horizons with a proper volatility-scaled construction may partially close the gap through diversification within the momentum-horizon space. The 1985–2012 Hurst et al. sample is the evidence base; post-2012 shifts in trend persistence at different horizons may alter the gradient.

The smile pattern reflects the strategy design: TSMOM profits most when assets trend consistently in one direction over the formation period, which occurs most reliably during sustained directional moves. The near-zero equity correlation confirms that TSMOM is not a directional equity bet but a conditional diversifier. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010) Figure 2. tsmom_returns_by_equity_market_decile; sp500_correlation_unconditional; trailing_equity_return; tsmom_conditional_sharpe The smile pattern is consistent with the Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012) finding of best TSMOM performance in extreme market months. The near-zero equity correlation (~-0.02) combined with the smile pattern makes TSMOM a particularly valuable crisis hedge: it tends to perform best precisely when equity portfolios suffer most, although this is a conditional (not guaranteed) property. Identification requires decile-conditional return analysis, not just an unconditional correlation.

After controlling for a simple diversified time-series momentum factor, the net-of-fee alpha of every managed futures fund in the sample becomes negative. A 2-and-20 fee structure (2% management fee, 20% performance fee) applied to the diversified TSMOM strategy implies an average annual fee load of approximately 6% on the gross return, which exceeds the alpha individual managers generate beyond the systematic trend signal. Section IV of Hurst et al. (2013) regresses individual managed futures fund net returns on the diversified TSMOM factor. Pre-fee, funds show positive but modest alpha; post-fee, all funds show negative alpha. The paper estimates the fee load by simulating 2-and-20 on the TSMOM gross return series, finding ~6% average annual fee drag. High R-squared values (0.36–0.64) confirm that TSMOM explains most managed futures return variation.

A diversified time-series momentum strategy across 58 liquid futures contracts achieves a gross annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 1.8 at a 10% annualized volatility target, over the period January 1985 through June 2012. This represents a substantial diversification benefit over the individual asset average Sharpe of 0.38 (12-month horizon). Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013) Table 2 and Section III report the diversified TSMOM portfolio performance. The portfolio volatility-scales each of the 58 positions to a common ex-ante 10% annual volatility, then combines them equally. The resulting Sharpe of ~1.8 (gross) reflects cross-asset diversification. The paper uses this as the benchmark replication of managed futures industry returns.

For individual assets, the Sharpe ratio of a time-series momentum strategy increases monotonically with the signal look-back horizon across the 1-month, 3-month, and 12-month horizons: 0.29, 0.36, and 0.38 respectively, averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts. Longer look-back horizons consistently outperform shorter look-back horizons at the individual asset level. Table 1 of Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013 JOIM / 2010 working paper) reports individual-instrument Sharpe ratios for TSMOM strategies with formation periods of 1 month, 3 months, and 12 months. Averages across all 58 instruments show the monotone horizon pattern. Authors note the 12-month signal dominates in the individual asset setting but that diversification benefits are largest at shorter horizons.

Most managed futures managers in the sample weight medium- to long-term trend signals (3-month horizon dominant) and systematically overweight fixed income relative to the equal-volatility benchmark. The typical manager's signal mix more closely resembles a 3-month TSMOM factor than a 12-month one, despite the 12-month signal having the highest individual-asset Sharpe ratio. Section IV.B of Hurst et al. (2013) decomposes the exposures of individual managed futures funds to TSMOM factors at 1m, 3m, and 12m horizons. The factor loading analysis shows that the 3-month TSMOM factor has the highest average loading across funds, suggesting most CTAs operate in the medium-term trend space. Asset class analysis shows above-benchmark fixed income weights (bonds and rates) in the typical fund.

Time-series momentum exhibits a "smile" return pattern: it performs best during prolonged bear or bull market environments and worst during trendless, choppy markets. Over the full 1985–2012 sample, TSMOM has near-zero correlation with the S&P 500 (approximately -0.02), confirming that the strategy is not a directional equity bet. Figure 2 and Section III.B of Hurst et al. (2013) analyze TSMOM returns conditional on trailing equity market returns and market volatility. The smile pattern emerges from the strategy's design: TSMOM profits most when assets trend consistently in one direction over the formation period, which occurs most reliably during sustained bull or bear markets. The near-zero S&P correlation is calculated from the full monthly return series.

risk_control The ~4.7x diversification benefit (individual-asset Sharpe 0.38 → diversified portfolio Sharpe 1.8 gross) documented by Hurst et al. (2013) implies that concentration in a subset of the 58-instrument universe materially degrades risk-adjusted returns. Risk control features: (1) instrument-count tracker— reducing the active instrument count below ~40 of the 58-instrument benchmark will erode a disproportionate share of the diversification premium; (2) asset class coverage indicator—equal representation across the four asset classes (commodities, equities, bonds, currencies) is required to capture the full diversification benefit; missing asset classes should trigger risk alerts; (3) volatility concentration metric—verify that no single instrument or asset class accounts for more than 30–35% of total portfolio volatility, consistent with a well-diversified 10%-vol-target-per-instrument construction; (4) S&P 500 correlation monitor—near-zero unconditional correlation (~-0.02) is the risk neutrality benchmark; positive correlation spikes signal unintended equity factor loading. Model the diversified TSMOM benchmark gross Sharpe (~1.8) as the target achievable only with a full multi-asset futures universe (58+ liquid instruments). Concentrated implementations (e.g., equities-only or commodities-only TSMOM) should be expected to produce Sharpe ratios substantially below 1.8, closer to the individual-asset average of 0.38. Risk controls should enforce minimum asset-class breadth requirements and track the diversification ratio as a forward-looking Sharpe degradation indicator when instruments are dropped from the universe. Confidence in achieving gross Sharpe near 1.8 requires: (1) all four asset classes represented with approximately equal volatility contribution; (2) active instrument count above 40; (3) near-zero S&P 500 correlation. Deviations from any of these conditions should trigger proportional reductions in expected Sharpe from the 1.8 benchmark. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe at 10% vol target is a full-universe, equal-volatility- weighted benchmark. It is gross of fees; after typical 2-and-20 managed futures fee structures, net Sharpe is substantially lower (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003). The 10%-per-instrument volatility target methodology normalizes position sizes across diverse asset classes; deviations from this normalization will produce concentration that degrades the diversification benefit.

confidence_calibration Confidence calibration for managed futures fund returns must account for the ~6% average annual fee drag under 2-and-20 structures, as documented by Hurst et al. (2013). The fee calibration features are: (1) fund-level fee structure identifier—management fee percentage plus performance fee percentage; (2) gross-to-net return conversion applying the documented 2% management fee plus 20% performance fee to the TSMOM gross return series; (3) TSMOM R-squared for each fund return series (0.36–0.64 range documented)—funds with higher R-squared are more TSMOM-driven and thus more susceptible to complete fee erosion of systematic alpha; (4) post-fee alpha relative to the TSMOM factor— the primary evidence metric, which is negative for all documented funds under 2-and-20 after TSMOM factor control. When classifying managed futures fund returns as evidence for the trend-following state, apply a fee-adjusted confidence weighting: gross TSMOM performance (~1.8 Sharpe) is strong evidence for the underlying trend-following state, but managed futures fund net performance is not an independent confirmation. After controlling for the TSMOM factor and deducting ~6% annual fee load, fund net alpha is negative—indicating no incremental information about trend-following state strength beyond what the systematic TSMOM factor already captures. Confidence in the underlying trend-following state should be calibrated to the gross systematic TSMOM factor performance, not to managed fund net returns. Do not use managed futures fund net-of-fee returns as confirmation of the trend-following state's activity. Use the diversified TSMOM factor gross return (targeting ~1.8 Sharpe at 10% vol) as the state indicator. Managed fund net returns understate state strength due to fee extraction; gross factor performance overstates achievable net investor return. Calibrate investor-accessible expected return at the lower-fee implementation level (e.g., systematic rules-based fund with ~0.5–1% expense ratio rather than 2-and-20). The 6% average annual fee load estimate is approximate and derived by simulating 2% management plus 20% performance fee on the TSMOM gross return series (Hurst et al., Section IV). Actual fee loads vary by fund and period; the documented range of R-squared (0.36–0.64) means funds with higher TSMOM beta will have proportionally higher systematic fee drag. The policy conclusion (use systematic low-cost TSMOM exposure rather than managed fund vehicles to access the trend premium) follows directly from the fee analysis but is a policy interpretation, not a direct stated conclusion of the paper.

activity_suppression The smile pattern of TSMOM returns documented by Hurst et al. (2013)—best performance during sustained bull and bear markets, worst during trendless choppy markets—implies that activity should be conditioned on the current equity market regime. Features for regime-conditional TSMOM activity: (1) trailing equity market return over 3–12 months as a regime indicator— directional markets (strong positive or strong negative trailing returns) correspond to the "smile tails" where TSMOM performs best; (2) equity market volatility regime indicator—high volatility combined with low directional trend (choppy regime) signals the worst environment for TSMOM; (3) conditional return decile rank of trailing equity return—TSMOM performs best in the top and bottom deciles, worst in the middle deciles; (4) S&P 500 unconditional correlation monitor (~-0.02 target)—a significant positive deviation signals unintended directional equity exposure that may distort the smile pattern. Do not assume TSMOM delivers uniform returns across market regimes. Condition model confidence and signal weighting on the current equity market regime: increase TSMOM signal weight during sustained directional regimes (top or bottom decile of trailing equity returns) and reduce weight during choppy indeterminate regimes. The 1.8 gross Sharpe is an unconditional average; regime-conditional expected Sharpe varies substantially above and below this level. Near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02) is the target; sustained positive correlation indicates the portfolio has drifted from its diversifying character. Confidence in TSMOM state returns is highest in sustained directional market environments (both bull and bear, consistent with the smile tails). Reduce confidence in trendless or high-volatility choppy regimes where TSMOM historically shows near-zero or negative returns. Activity suppression is warranted in confirmed choppy regimes where trailing equity return occupies the middle deciles for 3+ consecutive months. Suppress full TSMOM activity allocation when the trailing equity market return occupies middle deciles (approximately 4th through 7th deciles) for sustained periods (3+ months), signaling a trendless choppy regime inconsistent with the smile pattern's optimal conditions. Maintain reduced-activity (not zero) allocation to preserve exposure for the transition back to a sustained directional regime, as the smile pattern requires maintained positioning to benefit from sudden trend emergence. The smile pattern is a conditional average, not a regime classifier with a sharp entry/exit threshold. The practical implication is proportional weighting adjustment rather than binary on/off switching. The near-zero S&P 500 unconditional correlation (~-0.02) applies over the full 1985–2012 sample; within the smile pattern, TSMOM is positively correlated to equities during bull markets (both moving in the same direction) and negatively correlated during bear markets (where TSMOM profits from short positions).

model_weighting When the multi-asset trend following state is classified as active, emphasize: (1) diversified TSMOM signals across all available asset classes (commodities, equities, fixed income, currencies) to capture the ~4.7x diversification benefit relative to individual-asset Sharpe; (2) volatility-scaled position sizing per instrument (target 10% annualized vol per instrument before combination, consistent with the Hurst et al. benchmark methodology); (3) smile-pattern conditioning: weight TSMOM signals more heavily when trailing equity market returns indicate a sustained directional regime (both bull and bear tails), and reduce weight in trendless high-volatility environments. De-emphasize TSMOM signals when the market is in a mean- reverting choppy regime incompatible with sustained directional moves. The gross diversified TSMOM Sharpe of ~1.8 (January 1985–June 2012) is the benchmark for a fully diversified implementation with proper volatility scaling. Models should not use individual-asset Sharpe ratios (0.29–0.38) as the expected portfolio Sharpe; the diversification benefit is essential. After applying 2-and-20 fee structures, the net-of-fee alpha becomes negative (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003); a low-cost systematic implementation (e.g., factor-based) is required to capture meaningful net investor return. Highest confidence in the TSMOM state when: the equity market is in a sustained directional regime (consistent with the smile pattern); the portfolio is diversified across all four asset classes with proper vol-scaling; and implementation costs are below the 6% annual fee-load threshold that eliminates net alpha. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe is computed over January 1985–June 2012 (a 27-year sample dominated by a secular bond bull market and multiple sustained equity bear and bull markets). The volatility target normalization (10% per instrument) is central to achieving the diversification benefit; without it, single-asset concentration dominates. Near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02) is the key portfolio construction argument for institutional allocation.

feature_selection Horizon selection for TSMOM signals should be governed by individual-asset Sharpe evidence (12-month dominant at 0.38) rather than by observed manager allocations (3-month dominant in CTA databases). The typical CTA horizon bias toward 3-month signals reflects capacity constraints and operational factors, not a superior signal horizon at moderate AUM. Policy for feature construction: (1) weight the 12-month look-back most heavily in the signal composite for strategies operating below institutional capacity limits; (2) include shorter-horizon signals (1-month, 3-month) for diversification within the momentum-horizon space; (3) monitor whether capacity pressure forces migration toward shorter horizons (reducing individual-asset Sharpe from 0.38 toward 0.29) as AUM scales; (4) avoid systematic fixed income overweight inherited from typical CTA factor exposures during the secular bond bull market period. Model the multi-asset TSMOM state with horizon-weighted signal construction favoring 12-month signals at the individual-asset level (Sharpe 0.38 vs. 0.29 and 0.36 for 1m and 3m). At the portfolio level, the diversification benefit largely equalizes horizon differences; the primary horizon choice matters most for individual-instrument signal quality. Separately model the manager-allocation landscape (typically 3-month dominant) versus the empirically optimal allocation (12-month dominant) to correctly attribute observed CTA returns to the factor mix. When CTA fund exposures are predominantly 3-month-horizon, expect gross Sharpe below the theoretically achievable 0.38 individual-asset benchmark. Confidence in maximum-Sharpe signal construction requires empirical confirmation that 12-month dominance has not been arbitraged away in the post-2012 period. The policy recommendation to emphasize 12-month signals applies specifically to the empirical context of Hurst et al. (2013) using 58 liquid futures contracts over 1985–2012. Post-2012 evidence should be used to recalibrate the optimal horizon given potential changes in market efficiency. The fixed income overweight in typical CTAs was beneficial during the secular bond bull market; this tailwind may not persist under rising rate environments.

The trend-following momentum state delivers robust gross returns but fails to generate positive net-of-fee alpha for investors in managed futures funds under standard 2-and-20 fee structures. After controlling for a simple diversified time-series momentum factor, every managed futures fund in the Hurst et al. (2013) sample shows negative net-of-fee alpha; the average annual fee drag under a 2% management fee plus 20% performance fee applied to the TSMOM gross return series is approximately 6% per year. High R-squared values of 0.36–0.64 confirm that the TSMOM factor explains the majority of managed futures return variation, leaving little room for manager skill-based alpha net of costs. A model that uses gross TSMOM Sharpe ratios (~1.8) without fee adjustment overestimates net investor return by approximately 6 percentage points per year, confusing the availability of the underlying trend premium with the value-add of managed fund vehicles as delivery mechanisms for that premium. When managed futures fund gross returns are used without deducting the ~6% average annual fee load under 2-and-20 structures; when manager selection is premised on gross alpha rather than post-fee alpha; when the TSMOM systematic factor is not controlled for in performance attribution; when the R-squared of fund returns on the TSMOM factor (0.36–0.64) is not accounted for in skill-based interpretation. The finding that all funds show negative net-of-fee alpha does not mean trend following is unprofitable; it means that the fee structure transfers the majority of the systematic trend premium from investors to managers. A lower-fee vehicle (e.g., a systematic rules-based trend ETF with ~0.5% expense ratio) capturing the same TSMOM exposure would preserve most of the gross ~1.8 Sharpe benefit for end investors. The 6% average fee load is approximate and varies with the specific gross return realization in each period.

Managed futures managers systematically underexpose their portfolios to the individually optimal 12-month look-back horizon signal, operating predominantly at the 3-month horizon, and overweight fixed income relative to a balanced equal-volatility multi-asset benchmark. Factor loading analysis of CTA fund returns against 1m, 3m, and 12m TSMOM factors shows the 3-month factor carries the highest average loading across funds, despite the 12-month signal achieving the highest individual-asset Sharpe (0.38 vs 0.29 and 0.36). The systematic underweighting of the 12-month signal means managers collectively leave Sharpe ratio on the table relative to the empirical optimum. Additionally, the fixed income overweight (above equal-volatility benchmark levels) exposes the typical CTA portfolio to a secular bond market tailwind during the 1985–2012 sample period that may not persist. A model treating managed futures fund exposures as representative of the optimal TSMOM signal mix will misclassify the active horizon allocation as evidence that 3-month is the superior horizon, when it instead reflects behavioral and operational biases. When CTA fund factor loadings are used to infer the optimal TSMOM signal horizon mix rather than the horizon that maximizes Sharpe; when the fixed income overweight in typical CTA portfolios is not adjusted for secular bond bull market tailwinds during the estimation period (1985–2012); when manager horizon selection is interpreted as reflecting signal quality rather than capacity constraints, AUM-driven turnover limits, or client preferences for lower volatility (shorter-horizon signals have lower individual Sharpes but may have lower tail risk in certain regimes). The medium-term (3-month) dominance in CTA exposures may reflect rational capacity management: longer-horizon signals require larger position sizes in given instruments and are harder to scale without market impact at large AUM. Shorter-horizon signals offer higher turnover but lower capacity. The optimal horizon in practice depends on AUM, instrument liquidity, and execution costs—factors not captured by the gross Sharpe comparison.

Portfolios constructed with a dominant 1-month TSMOM signal (individual-asset Sharpe 0.29) systematically underperform those using a 12-month dominant signal (Sharpe 0.38), leaving approximately 0.09 Sharpe ratio units on the table at the individual-asset level before diversification. The monotone gradient from Hurst et al. (2013)—SR 0.29 (1m), 0.36 (3m), 0.38 (12m) averaged across 58 liquid futures—implies that every unit of signal weight shifted from longer to shorter horizons at the individual-instrument level degrades expected gross Sharpe in proportion to that weight shift. A model that assigns equal horizon weights (1/3 to each of 1m, 3m, 12m) without adjusting for the empirical gradient will underestimate achievable Sharpe by approximately 0.04–0.05 units relative to the 12m-dominant weighted optimum. This failure is distinct from the manager horizon bias failure (failure_hurst_mf_horizon_bias_005): here, the failure is in model design (choosing a suboptimal horizon weighting scheme), not in practitioner behavior. The failure is most consequential at moderate AUM where capacity constraints do not yet force migration to shorter horizons. When TSMOM signal construction assigns equal or higher weight to 1-month or 3-month horizons than to the 12-month horizon without capacity-driven justification; when the horizon-Sharpe gradient (0.29/0.36/0.38) is not used to inform signal weighting; when shorter-horizon signals are added for diversification benefit without confirming that the diversification gain outweighs the individual-asset Sharpe reduction; when the dominant CTA horizon allocation (3-month heavy, as documented by Hurst et al.) is adopted as the default without checking whether the operational justifications (AUM capacity, client expectations) apply to the modeled strategy. The failure is most clearly expressed at the individual-asset level (SR 0.29 vs 0.38 over the 58-instrument average). At the diversified portfolio level, combining all three horizons with a proper volatility-scaled construction may partially close the gap through diversification within the momentum-horizon space. The 1985–2012 Hurst et al. sample is the evidence base; post-2012 shifts in trend persistence at different horizons may alter the gradient.

entries.state_summary: Multi-Asset Time-Series Momentum Trend Following State. A market condition in which time-series momentum (TSMOM) signals deliver persistent risk-adjusted excess returns across diversified multi-asset futures portfolios. Characterized by: (1) individual-asset Sharpe ratios that increase monotonically with signal look-back horizon—0.29 (1-month), 0.36 (3-month), 0.38 (12-month)—averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts; (2) a diversified 58-instrument TSMOM portfolio achieving ~1.8 gross annualized Sharpe at 10% vol target (January 1985–June 2012); (3) a "smile" return pattern—best performance in sustained trending environments (strong bull or bear markets), worst in trendless choppy markets—with near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02); (4) after controlling for a simple diversified TSMOM factor, all managed futures fund net-of-fee alphas become negative under 2-and-20 fee structures (~6% average annual fee drag). Most CTAs exhibit dominant exposure to the 3-month TSMOM signal rather than the individually optimal 12-month horizon, and systematically overweight fixed income. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010), evidence_tier 2 (practitioner paper with direct empirical content).
