[state] Short-Horizon Weekly Return Predictability State. A market condition in which weekly equity portfolio returns exhibit significant positive first-order autocorrelation, strongly rejecting the random walk hypothesis. Characterized by variance ratio VR(2) ≈ 1.30 for the equal-weighted CRSP NYSE/AMEX index (implying first-order autocorrelation ρ(1) ≈ 0.30) over the full 1962–1985 sample; z-statistics of 7.18 to 18.46 for equal-weighted portfolios and 3.84 for value-weighted under the homoscedastic null—robust to heteroscedasticity (z* statistics also highly significant). The autocorrelation is strongly increasing in the inverse of market capitalization: smallest-cap quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.42 (up to 0.51 in 1974–1979), largest-cap quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.14. Non-synchronous trading alone cannot explain the magnitude: at a 10% daily non-trading probability (empirically realistic) induced weekly portfolio autocorrelation is only ≈ 2.3%; at an extreme 50% non-trading frequency it reaches at most 22%—insufficient to explain observed 30–42%. The pattern is consistent with returns-fads (persistent but mean-reverting return components from gradual information diffusion), not price fads (which would imply negative autocorrelation). Evidence from Lo and MacKinlay (1988), Journal of Finance, evidence_tier 1.
[signature_lo_mackinlay_fads_vr_profile_004] Observable returns-fads structure in weekly equity returns identified by the shape of the variance ratio profile VR(q) across aggregation horizons q = 2, 4, 8, 16 weeks, providing a qualitative discriminator between returns fads (positive declining autocorrelation) and price fads (negative autocorrelation at longer lags). The signature is detectable as: (1) VR(q) > 1 for all q = 2, 4, 8, 16, with the excess above unity diminishing as q increases—reflecting positive but declining autocorrelation at increasing lags; (2) absence of VR(q) falling below 1.0 at any weekly aggregation horizon up to 16 weeks—which would indicate price fads or negative autocorrelation inconsistent with the observed pattern; (3) equal-weighted CRSP index showing VR(2) ≈ 1.30 (ρ(1) ≈ 0.15 per the VR decomposition) as the anchor, with VR(4) and VR(8) above unity but at decreasing increments; (4) the autocorrelation structure consistent with gradual information diffusion (under-reaction) where the positive autocorrelation at short lags dissipates without reverting to negative—contrasting with Poterba- Summers long-horizon mean reversion where autocorrelation does eventually turn negative at 3–8 year horizons. Evidence from Lo and MacKinlay (1988) Table 2 and Section III.B, CRSP 1962–1985. variance_ratio_q2; variance_ratio_q4; variance_ratio_q8; variance_ratio_q16; vr_profile_slope; weekly_autocorrelation_lag1; weekly_autocorrelation_lag2; weekly_autocorrelation_lag3 The returns-fads vs. price-fads distinction is theoretically important: returns fads imply an under-reaction mechanism (investors update prices gradually to news), while price fads imply overreaction and subsequent correction. The observed VR(q) profile for weekly equity returns supports returns fads over the 1–16 week horizon. At longer horizons (monthly to multi-year), the Poterba-Summers evidence shows the autocorrelation eventually turning negative—the two findings are compatible within an S-shaped price response model where short-horizon momentum and long-horizon mean reversion coexist. The VR(q) profile is the key measurement tool for distinguishing the two types of fads empirically.
[signature_lo_mackinlay_size_autocorr_gradient_003] Observable cross-sectional gradient of weekly return autocorrelation strongly increasing with the inverse of firm market capitalization, providing a size-conditional measure of the short-horizon predictability state. The signature is detectable as: (1) smallest-cap quintile portfolio ρ(1) ≈ 0.42 (full sample), reaching up to 0.51 in the 1974–1979 sub-period; (2) largest-cap quintile portfolio ρ(1) ≈ 0.14 (statistically significant but economically modest); (3) corresponding VR(2) values from approximately 1.84 (smallest quintile) to 1.28 (largest quintile); (4) at extreme non-trading probabilities of 50%—far exceeding any empirically plausible estimate—the induced portfolio autocorrelation is at most 0.22, leaving the observed 0.30–0.42 range unexplained by non-synchronous trading alone. The size gradient motivates small-cap-tilted short-horizon momentum strategies and confirms that the predictability state is most powerful in the micro-cap segment. Evidence from Lo and MacKinlay (1988) Tables 3–4. size_quintile_vr2_smallest; size_quintile_vr2_largest; autocorrelation_lag1_small_cap; autocorrelation_lag1_large_cap; non_trading_probability; induced_autocorrelation_bound The size-autocorrelation gradient is consistent with non-synchronous trading (small stocks trade less frequently) contributing a portion of the measured autocorrelation, but Lo-MacKinlay's bounding analysis establishes that non-trading alone is quantitatively insufficient even at extreme probabilities (50%). The residual genuine autocorrelation post non-trading adjustment points to lead-lag effects, investor under-reaction, or microstructure friction. The gradient has direct implications for small-cap momentum strategy design.
[signature_lo_mackinlay_variance_ratio_001] Observable excess variance ratio above unity and statistically significant positive first-order autocorrelation in weekly equity portfolio returns, providing a direct quantitative signal of short-horizon return predictability. The signature is measurable as: (1) variance ratio VR(2) ≈ 1.30 for the equal-weighted CRSP NYSE/AMEX index, implying ρ(1) ≈ 0.30 via VR(2) = 1 + 2ρ(1); (2) z-statistics of 7.18–18.46 for equal-weighted portfolios and 3.84 for the value-weighted index under the homoscedastic null; (3) z* statistics (heteroscedasticity-consistent) also highly significant, ruling out ARCH-type variance dynamics as the sole explanation; (4) sub-period stability: VR(2) ranges from 1.27 to 1.38 across four 1962–1985 sub-periods. The pattern is consistent with returns-fads (declining positive autocorrelation at increasing lags, i.e., VR(q) increasing but at a decreasing rate as q grows from 2 to 16), not price fads (which would require negative autocorrelation at longer lags). Evidence from Lo and MacKinlay (1988), Journal of Finance, evidence_tier 1. variance_ratio_q2; variance_ratio_q4; variance_ratio_q8; variance_ratio_q16; z_statistic_homoscedastic; z_star_heteroscedastic; weekly_autocorrelation_lag1; equal_weighted_index_return; value_weighted_index_return VR(q) = 1 + 2Σ_{k=1}^{q-1}(1-k/q)ρ(k); the simple VR(2) ≈ 1 + 2ρ(1) relationship gives the first-order autocorrelation approximately. The z-stat range of 7–18 effectively rules out sampling error; rejection of the random walk is decisive. The index-level autocorrelation (30%) far exceeds individual stock autocorrelation due to lead-lag effects among large and small stocks. The returns-fads interpretation (positive declining autocorrelation) contrasts with the Poterba-Summers long-horizon mean reversion finding (negative autocorrelation at 3–8 years); the two are empirically compatible.
[claim_lo_mackinlay_ew_autocorrelation_002] The first-order weekly autocorrelation of the equal-weighted CRSP NYSE/AMEX index return is approximately 30% (variance ratio at q=2 of approximately 1.30) over the full 1962–1985 sample. This is economically and statistically large: a 30% positive autocorrelation implies that roughly 30% of this week's return is predictable from last week's return. Table 2 of Lo and MacKinlay (1988) reports VR(q) for q = 2, 4, 8, 16 for the equal-weighted CRSP index over the full sample. VR(2) ≈ 1.30 for the full period; VR(2) values range from approximately 1.27 to 1.38 across sub-periods. The equal-weighted index first-order autocorrelation coefficient ρ̂(1) is approximately 0.30 under the relationship VR(2) ≈ 1 + 2ρ̂(1).
[claim_lo_mackinlay_nontrading_bound_005] Non-synchronous trading can induce spurious positive autocorrelation in portfolio returns, but at empirically realistic non-trading probabilities it accounts for only a small fraction of the observed autocorrelation. [claim_lo_mackinlay_returns_fads_004] The observed pattern of positive, declining autocorrelation at increasing weekly lags is consistent with "returns fads" (transitory price deviations that eventually revert) but inconsistent with "price fads." For value-weighted portfolios, the z=3.84 rejection is strong but the effect size is smaller; random-walk assumptions should receive low but non-zero weight. Sub-period stability (VR(2) range 1.27–1.38) supports treating the rejection as robust across the sample period, not as an artifact of a specific sub-period. The z-statistics of 7–18 effectively rule out type-I sampling error; the random walk is not merely borderline-rejected but overwhelmingly rejected for equal- weighted portfolios. This means random-walk-based efficiency arguments carry essentially no weight for equal-weighted short-horizon equity model components. The policy is to down-weight, not to fully suppress, random-walk model components for value-weighted portfolios given the smaller but still significant z=3.84.

confidence_calibration Application of non-trading corrections to observed weekly return autocorrelation must be bounded by the Lo-MacKinlay (1988) analytical limits to avoid overcorrection. The correction calibration features are: (1) empirical daily non-trading probability estimate per stock or portfolio constituent—the realistic range is approximately 5–15% for NYSE stocks in the sample period; (2) the implied upper bound on non-trading-induced autocorrelation at realistic probabilities: approximately 2.3% at 10% daily non-trading frequency, 22% at the extreme 50% frequency; (3) residual autocorrelation after non-trading correction: even at the extreme 50% bound, the corrected equal-weighted index autocorrelation is approximately 0.30 − 0.22 = 0.08 or higher, remaining material and statistically significant; (4) maximum plausible non-trading adjustment as a feature cap—any non-trading correction that would reduce the observed autocorrelation to below the 22% maximum bound should be flagged as methodologically unsupported. When applying non-trading corrections to measured weekly return autocorrelation, the maximum credible correction at empirically realistic parameters is ~2.3% (10% non-trading probability). At no empirically plausible calibration does non-trading explain more than 22% of the observed 30–42% autocorrelation. After any legitimate non-trading correction, the residual autocorrelation remains material and directionally consistent with genuine predictability. Do not apply corrections that reduce measured autocorrelation to near zero; such corrections are not supported by the Lo-MacKinlay bounding analysis and imply an empirically implausible non-trading frequency. Confidence in genuine return predictability (beyond microstructure noise) should remain high after a legitimate non-trading correction. The non-trading bound result (claim_lo_mackinlay_nontrading_bound_005) establishes that at least ~8–28 percentage points of the observed 30–42% autocorrelation reflects genuine predictability after maximum plausible non-trading adjustment. Methodologies that apply non-trading corrections exceeding the 22% upper bound should be treated as overcorrecting and producing spuriously low residual autocorrelation. The Lo-MacKinlay non-trading bound analysis derives closed-form expressions for the autocorrelation induced purely by non-synchronous trading, showing the induced autocorrelation is a function of the daily non-trading probability. The 10% and 50% probability examples bracket the empirically relevant range; at 10% (realistic), the induced autocorrelation is only 2.3%—essentially negligible relative to the observed 30%. This analysis is a falsification of the hypothesis that non-trading alone explains observed short-horizon autocorrelation.

feature_selection When the short-horizon return predictability state is active (weekly autocorrelation statistically significant and VR(2) > 1.0 for equal-weighted portfolios), emphasize: (1) lagged weekly return features for portfolio-level predictions, particularly for equal-weighted indices and small-cap portfolios where ρ(1) is largest (0.30–0.42); (2) variance ratio features computed at q = 2, 4, 8 weeks as state-activity indicators; (3) returns-fads structure indicators (VR(q) profile across q showing declining incremental autocorrelation at longer lags). De-emphasize random-walk-based features that assume zero short-horizon autocorrelation. Non-trading microstructure corrections should not remove the full autocorrelation signal, as Lo-MacKinlay's bounding analysis shows non-trading accounts for at most 2.3–22% of the observed 30–42% autocorrelation at realistic to extreme non-trading frequencies. Calibrate short-horizon momentum models using the empirical autocorrelation magnitudes: equal-weighted index ρ(1) ≈ 0.30, value-weighted ρ(1) < 0.14. The z-statistics of 7–18 for equal-weighted portfolios confirm that sampling error cannot explain the autocorrelation signal at any conventional significance level. Models should not apply non-trading corrections that would reduce the autocorrelation estimate to near zero; the corrected autocorrelation remains material and statistically significant even after the empirically appropriate non-trading adjustment. High confidence in the short-horizon predictability state for equal-weighted and small-cap portfolios. Moderate confidence for value-weighted or large-cap portfolios (ρ(1) ≈ 0.14, statistically significant but economically smaller). Confidence is not dependent on rejecting all microstructure explanations; the non-trading bound result establishes that genuine predictability survives any empirically realistic adjustment. The equal-weighted index autocorrelation (30%) primarily reflects lead-lag effects between large-cap (information leaders) and small-cap (laggards) stocks, not individual stock autocorrelation. Individual stock autocorrelations are much lower and often statistically insignificant. The policy is applicable to portfolio-level strategies, not stock-picking based on individual serial correlation. The 1962–1985 sample period is the evidence base; post-sample stability should be verified before applying the calibrated magnitudes.

position_sizing Size-based position sizing should reflect the empirically documented autocorrelation gradient: short-horizon return predictability is strongest in the smallest market-cap quintile (ρ(1) ≈ 0.42) and weakest in the largest quintile (ρ(1) ≈ 0.14). Features for a size-conditional strategy: (1) market- cap quintile classification of portfolio constituents; (2) size-conditional variance ratio VR(2) computed per quintile (ranging from ~1.84 to ~1.28); (3) sub-period stability of size-autocorrelation gradient (smallest quintile reaches 0.51 in 1974–1979, confirming it is not sample-specific). The gradient implies that small-cap portfolios warrant larger position sizes per unit of autocorrelation signal than large-cap portfolios, assuming the mechanism (lead-lag effects) remains active. Scale position sizes for short-horizon momentum strategies proportionally to the autocorrelation estimate for the relevant size tier. Do not apply a uniform autocorrelation assumption across all cap-size strata; the 3x gradient from largest to smallest quintile (0.14 vs 0.42) is material for expected returns and should be reflected in signal weights. The non-trading bound result confirms that at least a majority of the small-cap autocorrelation (42% observed vs. ≤22% non-trading bound at extreme) reflects genuine predictability rather than microstructure friction alone. Size tilt confidence is highest for the smallest market-cap quintile where autocorrelation is largest and most robustly documented. The predictability gradient narrows from 0.42 to 0.14 across quintiles; confidence decreases monotonically from small-cap toward large-cap within a short-horizon strategy. Apply non-trading corrections only at magnitudes consistent with the 2.3% (10% non-trading probability) to 22% (50% non-trading probability) bound; corrections larger than this are not supported by Lo-MacKinlay's bounding analysis. The size-autocorrelation gradient has direct practical implications for portfolio construction in short-horizon momentum strategies: overweight the smallest-cap strata where the signal is strongest. However, small-cap implementation faces liquidity constraints and higher transaction costs; the net signal after cost adjustment may be more uniform across cap tiers than the gross gradient implies. Transaction cost verification is required before operationalizing the size tilt.

Models that attribute the observed short-horizon weekly return autocorrelation primarily or entirely to non-synchronous trading (non-trading days inducing spurious autocorrelation) will systematically overestimate the microstructure component and underestimate genuine return predictability. Lo and MacKinlay (1988) derive closed-form bounds showing that at a 10% daily non-trading probability—consistent with empirical estimates for NYSE stocks—the induced weekly portfolio autocorrelation is only approximately 2.3%. Even at an extreme and empirically implausible 50% non-trading probability, the induced autocorrelation reaches at most 22%; the observed equal-weighted index autocorrelation of 30–42% exceeds this bound. Non-trading is insufficient to explain the observed autocorrelation magnitude at any realistic calibration. A model that "corrects" the observed VR(2) using a non-trading adjustment calibrated at realistic frequencies will find the corrected autocorrelation remains large and statistically significant, not approximately zero. Models premised on non-trading as the dominant driver will fail to produce the observed returns-fads pattern (positive declining autocorrelation at increasing lags). When the full observed weekly autocorrelation (ρ(1) ≈ 0.30–0.42) is attributed primarily to non-synchronous trading; when correction methods assume that non-trading accounts for the majority of autocorrelation; when the Scholes-Williams (1977) or Cohen et al. (1983) non-trading corrections are applied without checking that residual autocorrelation remains unexplained; when a 10% non-trading probability is used to justify a 2.3% spurious autocorrelation claim that leaves 27+ percentage points unaccounted for. The non-trading bounding result shifts the burden of explanation to genuine return predictability or other microstructure sources (bid-ask bounce, order flow). Neither bid-ask bounce nor order flow alone can explain index-level autocorrelation of 30–42% without also implying unrealistically large trading costs. The lead-lag explanation (large stocks leading small stocks) is the empirically supported remaining mechanism, validated in Lo and MacKinlay (1990).

The size-autocorrelation gradient documented by Lo and MacKinlay (1988)—with the smallest market-cap quintile exhibiting ρ(1) ≈ 0.42 versus ρ(1) ≈ 0.14 for the largest quintile—is a gross (before-cost) predictability result; exploiting the strongest autocorrelation signal in the smallest-cap quintile requires accepting materially higher transaction costs, wider bid-ask spreads, and lower liquidity than available for the largest-cap quintile. A strategy that applies the 3x size-autocorrelation gradient (small vs. large) directly to position sizing without adjusting for the inverse relationship between firm size and market liquidity will overstate net-of-cost expected returns for small-cap momentum positions. Additionally, ρ(1) ≈ 0.42 for the smallest quintile (reaching 0.51 in 1974–1979) reflects a period when institutional trading activity and algorithmic execution were minimal; in more recent periods, improved information dissemination and electronic market-making have likely reduced the lead-lag effect generating small-cap autocorrelation, making the historical gradient an overestimate of the current gross signal. When position sizes in a short-horizon momentum strategy are scaled proportionally to autocorrelation magnitude across size quintiles without accounting for the liquidity-cost gradient; when the small-cap autocorrelation advantage (0.42 vs. 0.14) is applied to large-AUM strategies that face significant market impact costs in micro-cap stocks; when the 1962–1985 autocorrelation gradient is applied to post-2000 markets without adjusting for reduced information asymmetries and improved market microstructure in small-cap trading; when the sub-period peak (ρ(1) ≈ 0.51 in 1974–1979) is used as the primary calibration figure rather than the full-sample average (0.42). The size-autocorrelation gradient is a robust full-sample finding (1962–1985) but its exploitability depends critically on implementation costs. The non- trading bound analysis (claim_lo_mackinlay_nontrading_bound_005) shows that autocorrelation partially reflects microstructure friction rather than pure predictability; small-cap stocks have higher non-trading frequency, which contributes (but does not fully account for) the higher autocorrelation. Net-of-cost feasibility requires the gross autocorrelation advantage to exceed the incremental cost disadvantage—a condition not verified by Lo and MacKinlay (1988).

Using the value-weighted index autocorrelation (ρ(1) ≈ 0.14, VR(2) z=3.84) as the representative measure of short-horizon return predictability materially understates the strength of the predictability state as documented by Lo and MacKinlay (1988). The equal-weighted index autocorrelation ρ(1) ≈ 0.30 with z-statistics of 7.18–18.46 is approximately twice as large as the value-weighted estimate in both magnitude and z-score. A model calibrated using the value-weighted index as the primary benchmark will: (1) underestimate the strength of short- horizon autocorrelation in the overall CRSP universe by approximately 50–100%; (2) assign lower expected returns to short-horizon predictability signals than the equal-weighted evidence justifies; (3) underestimate the small-cap segment's contribution to total predictability signal, which is the largest component (smallest quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.42, largest quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.14). The value- weighted result is influenced by large-cap stocks, which exhibit lower but non-zero autocorrelation; the equal-weighted result better represents the breadth of the short-horizon predictability state across the full CRSP universe. When a value-weighted equity index is used as the representative benchmark for short-horizon return predictability calibration in contexts where equal-weighted exposure or small-cap tilting is feasible; when the ρ(1) ≈ 0.14 value-weighted autocorrelation is treated as the expected portfolio autocorrelation rather than as the large-cap subsegment estimate; when the z-statistic of 3.84 (value- weighted) is treated as representative of the rejection strength rather than the 7–18 range for equal-weighted portfolios; when the value-weighted result is used to argue that short-horizon predictability is borderline or modest when the equal-weighted evidence shows it to be decisive. The value-weighted vs. equal-weighted divergence arises from lead-lag effects: large-cap stocks respond to market-wide news first, and small-cap stocks follow in the next period. Value-weighting concentrates measurement in the information leaders (large-caps), which have lower autocorrelation because they respond quickly; equal-weighting captures the full cross-section including the laggards (small-caps), producing higher measured autocorrelation. The policy implication is to always report both weighted-index results and clarify which is being used as the primary calibration benchmark.

entries.state_summary: Short-Horizon Weekly Return Predictability State. A market condition in which weekly equity portfolio returns exhibit significant positive first-order autocorrelation, strongly rejecting the random walk hypothesis. Characterized by variance ratio VR(2) ≈ 1.30 for the equal-weighted CRSP NYSE/AMEX index (implying first-order autocorrelation ρ(1) ≈ 0.30) over the full 1962–1985 sample; z-statistics of 7.18 to 18.46 for equal-weighted portfolios and 3.84 for value-weighted under the homoscedastic null—robust to heteroscedasticity (z* statistics also highly significant). The autocorrelation is strongly increasing in the inverse of market capitalization: smallest-cap quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.42 (up to 0.51 in 1974–1979), largest-cap quintile ρ(1) ≈ 0.14. Non-synchronous trading alone cannot explain the magnitude: at a 10% daily non-trading probability (empirically realistic) induced weekly portfolio autocorrelation is only ≈ 2.3%; at an extreme 50% non-trading frequency it reaches at most 22%—insufficient to explain observed 30–42%. The pattern is consistent with returns-fads (persistent but mean-reverting return components from gradual information diffusion), not price fads (which would imply negative autocorrelation). Evidence from Lo and MacKinlay (1988), Journal of Finance, evidence_tier 1.

[state] Three-State HMM Market Regime (Bull / Bear / High-Volatility). A three-state hidden Markov model (HMM) regime structure applied asset- independently to daily futures returns across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income classes. The three states are labeled bull (positive return, moderate volatility), bear (negative or flat return, elevated volatility), and high-volatility (extreme variance). The model uses EWMM (exponentially weighted moving moment) features of first and second return moments, normalized and concatenated independently per instrument, as the observation vector. Applied uniformly to 15 futures instruments (4 commodity, 4 currency, 4 equity, 3 fixed income) using 4972 daily observations (January 2000 – October 2019). Three states selected via greedy model selection. The PESR metric (Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio) translates HMM-predicted state probabilities into a forward-looking scalar risk-adjusted return forecast by combining state-level SR estimates with h-step-ahead transition matrix powers. OOS long-only strategy (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019) achieves substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold across most instruments at 5bps transaction costs (e.g., EQ4: SR=3.0 vs. 1.0 B&H). EWMM span=30 provides a favorable SR/turnover tradeoff (Nguyen 2021 preprint).
[signature_nguyen_ewmm_span_calibration_001] The measured SR/turnover tradeoff profile as the EWMM span parameter s varies across candidate values {15, 30, 60}. At s=15, EWMM features are highly responsive to recent returns, producing frequent HMM regime transitions and high daily portfolio turnover (ranging approximately 1.64% to 4.87% for some instruments), which erodes net SR under realistic transaction costs. At s=30, the tradeoff is favorable: daily turnover averages approximately 2.54% for comparable instruments and OOS SR exceeds 1 for most of the 15 futures instruments. At s=60, excessive feature smoothing slows regime detection, causing the strategy to lag genuine regime shifts and reducing OOS SR. The observable signature is the SR/turnover tradeoff curve itself: a characteristic shape with a favorable interior region (approximately s=25 to s=45) and degradation at both extremes. This tradeoff is measurable from any rolling OOS backtest by varying span across a grid while holding all other model parameters fixed. Applicable uniformly across the 15 multi-asset futures instruments at 5bps transaction costs (Nguyen 2021, Sections 4.2, 5). ewmm_span_parameter; daily_portfolio_turnover; oos_sharpe_ratio_by_span; net_sr_after_transaction_costs The favorable span range (approximately s=25-45) is identified on OOS testing over 2016-2019 with 5bps transaction costs. The optimal span is expected to be cost-environment and instrument dependent: higher transaction costs will favor larger spans to reduce turnover; lower-latency execution may shift the optimal span toward lower values. The tradeoff curve is the primary diagnostic for span calibration; it should be re-evaluated when deploying to new instruments or substantially different cost environments. Source is a preprint.
[signature_nguyen_hmm_regime_states_001] The filtered probability distribution across three hidden Markov model states (bull, bear, high-volatility) estimated from EWMM features of daily futures returns. The observation vector per instrument is the concatenation of EWMM first moment (mean) and second moment (variance) of returns, normalized and processed independently per asset class. The three regime states correspond to distinct return-volatility configurations: bull (positive expected return, moderate volatility), bear (negative or near-zero expected return, elevated volatility), and high-volatility (extreme variance). The HMM filter produces real-time posterior state probability estimates that can be read as continuous regime indicators. Applied uniformly to 15 futures instruments (4 commodity, 4 currency, 4 equity, 3 fixed income; 4972 daily observations Jan 2000 – Oct 2019). Three states selected via greedy model selection (Nguyen 2021). hmm_filtered_state_probability_bull; hmm_filtered_state_probability_bear; hmm_filtered_state_probability_high_vol; ewmm_return_mean; ewmm_return_variance The asset-independent design is a key feature: the same HMM framework applies to commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income futures without modification. EWMM span parameter controls responsiveness (lower span = faster regime detection but higher turnover; span=30 recommended). Three-state structure identified via greedy approach; alternative state counts were not systematically validated.
[signature_nguyen_pesr_oos_sharpe_002] The Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio (PESR) scalar signal and associated out-of-sample risk-adjusted return performance across multi-asset futures. PESR is defined as PESR = (ESR)^T * alpha_{n+h|n}, where ESR_j is the state-level expected Sharpe ratio estimated from EWMM features in hidden state j, and alpha_{n+h|n} = alpha_{n|n} * A^h is the h-step-ahead predicted state probability vector computed by multiplying the current filtered state vector by the h-th power of the transition matrix A. PESR is a scalar forward-looking risk-adjusted return predictor; positions are set proportional to its sign and magnitude (long-only: max(0, PESR)). OOS long-only strategy (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019, span=30, 5bps transaction costs) achieves substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold for most of 15 futures instruments: EQ4 SR=3.0 vs. B&H 1.0; FI1 SR=1.91 vs. 0.27; CO1 SR=2.4 vs. 0.67 (Nguyen 2021, Tables 3-4). pesr_scalar_signal; hmm_predicted_state_probability_h_step; state_level_expected_sharpe_ratio; oos_sharpe_ratio; buy_and_hold_sharpe_ratio PESR is both the decision rule (translating regime probabilities into positions) and the performance signal (higher OOS SR when PESR accurately predicts regimes). OOS test period is relatively short (approximately 4 years, Jan 2016–Oct 2019). Source is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. The combination of preprint source and short OOS window warrants some evidence discount, though the magnitude of SR improvement across multiple asset classes is striking.
[claim_nguyen_oos_sharpe_003] In out-of-sample testing (January 2016 – October 2019), the HMM long-only strategy with EWMM span=30 achieves Sharpe ratios substantially above buy-and-hold for most instruments at 5bps transaction costs: EQ4 achieves SR=3.0 vs buy-and-hold SR=1.0, FI1 achieves SR=1.91 vs SR=0.27, and CO1 achieves SR=2.4 vs SR=0.67. Overall, span=30 produces SR>1 for most of the 15 instruments. Tables 3 and 4, p.5-6. Test period: Jan 2016 – Oct 2019 (approximately 4 years). Training: through 2012; validation: 2012-2016. Strategy is long- only with holdings capped at [0,1]. 5bps transaction cost per trade applied.
[claim_nguyen_pesr_metric_002] The Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio (PESR) metric is defined as PESR^S_i(h) = (ESR^S)^T * alpha_{n+h|n}, where ESR^S_j = mu_j(f_s^1) / mu_j(f_s^2) is the expected Sharpe ratio in hidden state j estimated from EWMM features, and alpha_{n+h|n} = alpha_{n|n} * A^h is the h-step-ahead state probability vector computed from the transition matrix. This scalar metric predicts risk-adjusted returns h steps ahead. Section 4.3 and Equation (4.1), p.4. The metric translates regime probabilities into a forward-looking SR forecast by combining state-level SR estimates with HMM-predicted state probabilities. Portfolio positions are set proportional to PESR sign and magnitude.
[claim_nguyen_span_tradeoff_004] The EWMM span parameter s controls regime stickiness: lower s makes features more responsive to recent data, increasing regime transition frequency and portfolio turnover; higher s smooths features more heavily, reducing turnover but slowing regime detection. Span s=30 corresponds to approximately 25-60 day rebalancing intervals and provides a favorable tradeoff between SR performance and transaction costs across most instruments. Sections 4.2 and 5, p.4-6. Spans s in {15, 30, 60} tested. Lower s increases the number of regime changes and thus turnover (daily turnover ranges roughly from 1.64% to 4.87% for s=15 vs. 2.54% for s=30 for some instruments). Higher s reduces responsiveness and may miss genuine regime shifts.
[claim_nguyen_three_state_hmm_001] A three-state hidden Markov model applied asset-independently to daily futures returns on 15 instruments across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income classes identifies three regimes labeled bull, bear, and high-volatility. The model uses EWMM features of first and second moments (mean and variance of returns) as the observation vector, normalized and concatenated for each instrument independently. Abstract and Sections 1, 2.1, 3, p.1-3. Data: 4972 daily closing return observations per instrument, January 2000 – October 2019. Three states chosen via greedy approach. The asset-independent design applies the same HMM framework to any asset class without modification.
[policy_nguyen_hmm_regime_switching_001] regime_switch Use EWMM features (first and second moments of daily returns with span=30) as inputs to a three-state HMM for real-time regime identification across multi- asset futures. The normalized EWMM observation vector is applicable across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income asset classes without modification, enabling a consistent cross-asset regime identification framework. HMM-filtered state probabilities (bull, bear, high-volatility) serve as the primary regime features for downstream position sizing and risk control. The three-state HMM (bull/bear/high-volatility) trained per instrument provides the regime state probability estimates used as model inputs. The PESR decision rule (PESR = ESR^T * alpha_{n+h|n}) translates h-step-ahead predicted regime probabilities into a scalar risk-adjusted return forecast. OOS evidence supports substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold for most of 15 futures instruments at 5bps transaction costs (Jan 2016–Oct 2019). Three-state structure selected via greedy approach; alternative state counts require validation before use in production. Confidence in HMM regime signal quality should be conditioned on EWMM span calibration: span=30 provides a favorable SR/turnover tradeoff in the OOS test period. High-confidence long positions are indicated when PESR is substantially positive; positions should be exited or reduced when PESR approaches zero or turns negative. Source is a preprint; confidence in robustness of OOS results requires corroboration from additional validation periods and asset classes. Suppress activity when HMM assigns high posterior probability to the high-volatility state (bear or high-vol dominant); reduce or close long positions when the predicted regime over the h-step horizon is unfavorable. OOS test period is approximately 4 years (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019); short window may not adequately capture multiple full market cycles. Results are from a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Long-only strategy design limits applicability to directional long strategies; extension to long/short requires separate validation. Transaction cost sensitivity should be tested at costs above 5bps.
[policy_nguyen_pesr_position_sizing_001] position_sizing Use the PESR scalar metric as the primary position-sizing signal for multi-asset futures strategies. PESR = (ESR)^T * alpha_{n+h|n} combines state-level Sharpe estimates with h-step-ahead predicted regime probabilities, providing a forward- looking risk-adjusted return forecast per instrument. EWMM span=30 is recommended as the baseline calibration for the EWMM features feeding the HMM (approximately 25-60 day rebalancing intervals, daily turnover ~2.54% for representative instruments in the OOS test period). Calibrate span on a validation period before production deployment. Position sizes in a long-only strategy should be set proportional to max(0, PESR); instruments with PESR>0 receive positive allocations, PESR<=0 instruments receive zero (no position). The h-step-ahead transition matrix power (A^h) determines forecast horizon; select h based on expected holding period and rebalancing frequency. The EWMM span controls the sensitivity/smoothness tradeoff: lower span increases position turnover; higher span increases detection lag. At 5bps transaction costs with span=30, OOS SR substantially exceeds buy-and-hold for most of 15 instruments (EQ4: 3.0 vs. 1.0; FI1: 1.91 vs. 0.27; CO1: 2.4 vs. 0.67). PESR magnitude provides a natural confidence signal: large positive PESR indicates high confidence in the bull state; PESR near zero indicates low confidence or regime uncertainty. Position size proportional to PESR magnitude implements implicit confidence-weighted scaling. Reduce positions when PESR is small in magnitude, reflecting mixed or uncertain regime signals. Zero positions when PESR<=0 (long-only mode). Consider reducing all position sizes proportionally when HMM assigns high posterior probability to the high-volatility state across multiple instruments simultaneously, as this may indicate a broad market stress episode. The PESR position sizing rule is definitional (evidence_tier=3); empirical performance evidence is in claim_nguyen_oos_sharpe_003. Span tradeoff evidence (evidence_tier=2) calibrates the key hyperparameter. Both the span calibration and OOS results are from a preprint on a short test window; the position sizing rule is well-designed but production deployment warrants additional validation on longer periods and real-time transaction cost estimates.
[failure_nguyen_hmm_state_count_001] The three-state HMM structure (bull, bear, high-volatility) was selected via a greedy model selection procedure applied uniformly across all 15 futures instruments. Greedy selection does not guarantee globally optimal state count and may produce suboptimal regime identification for instruments whose return dynamics are better described by a different number of states. For some instruments, a two-state model (bull/bear only) or a four-state model (with an additional low-volatility or trend-reversal state) may better capture the empirical return distribution. The uniform application of a single three-state architecture across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income futures ignores the possibility that different asset classes exhibit structurally different regime counts. Additionally, the same three-state labels (bull, bear, high-volatility) applied to all instruments may not have consistent economic interpretation across asset classes: a "bull" state in commodity futures differs materially from a "bull" state in fixed income futures. Misspecified state counts produce regime filter outputs that conflate distinct market conditions into merged states or split single conditions into spurious sub-states. When the three-state structure does not adequately capture the return dynamics of a specific instrument or asset class; when applying the model to instruments outside the training set of 15 futures contracts; when economic interpretation of state labels is required to be consistent across asset classes. The greedy selection procedure was not cross-validated on held-out instruments or time periods. The preprint does not report systematic model selection criteria (e.g., BIC, AIC, likelihood ratio tests) across different state counts to justify the three-state choice. Sensitivity analysis with two- and four-state variants would materially strengthen confidence in the three-state specification.
[failure_nguyen_oos_window_length_001] The out-of-sample test window used to validate the HMM long-only strategy (January 2016 – October 2019, approximately 4 years) is short and covers a predominantly bull-market phase for equities and a generally favorable period for trend-following in multiple asset classes. Sharpe ratio estimates derived from this OOS window may be upward biased due to favorable realized market conditions rather than genuine regime-detection alpha. The reported outperformance versus buy-and-hold (e.g., EQ4 SR=3.0 vs. 1.0) partially reflects both model skill and the specific market environment of the test period. A short OOS window spanning fewer than two full market cycles provides insufficient evidence to distinguish persistent regime-detection skill from favorable period selection. The strategy's performance during high-drawdown periods, bear markets, or structurally different volatility regimes remains undemonstrated by this test design. When OOS Sharpe ratio estimates from the 2016-2019 test period are extrapolated to other market environments without validation; when the reported OOS SR advantage is used as strong evidence of model robustness across full market cycles; when the approximately 4-year OOS window is treated as equivalent to multi-decade out-of-sample validation. The 2016-2019 test period includes the 2018 equity volatility spike and some trend disruption but largely misses a severe bear market test. linked_records.text: The measured SR/turnover tradeoff profile as the EWMM span parameter s varies across candidate values {15, 30, 60}. At s=15, EWMM features are highly responsive to recent returns, producing frequent HMM regime transitions and high daily portfolio turnover (ranging approximately 1.64% to 4.87% for some instruments), which erodes net SR under realistic transaction costs. At s=30, the tradeoff is favorable: daily turnover averages approximately 2.54% for comparable instruments and OOS SR exceeds 1 for most of the 15 futures instruments. At s=60, excessive feature smoothing slows regime detection, causing the strategy to lag genuine regime shifts and reducing OOS SR. The observable signature is the SR/turnover tradeoff curve itself: a characteristic shape with a favorable interior region (approximately s=25 to s=45) and degradation at both extremes. This tradeoff is measurable from any rolling OOS backtest by varying span across a grid while holding all other model parameters fixed. Applicable uniformly across the 15 multi-asset futures instruments at 5bps transaction costs (Nguyen 2021, Sections 4.2, 5). ewmm_span_parameter; daily_portfolio_turnover; oos_sharpe_ratio_by_span; net_sr_after_transaction_costs The favorable span range (approximately s=25-45) is identified on OOS testing over 2016-2019 with 5bps transaction costs. The optimal span is expected to be cost-environment and instrument dependent: higher transaction costs will favor larger spans to reduce turnover; lower-latency execution may shift the optimal span toward lower values. The tradeoff curve is the primary diagnostic for span calibration; it should be re-evaluated when deploying to new instruments or substantially different cost environments. Source is a preprint.

The filtered probability distribution across three hidden Markov model states (bull, bear, high-volatility) estimated from EWMM features of daily futures returns. The observation vector per instrument is the concatenation of EWMM first moment (mean) and second moment (variance) of returns, normalized and processed independently per asset class. The three regime states correspond to distinct return-volatility configurations: bull (positive expected return, moderate volatility), bear (negative or near-zero expected return, elevated volatility), and high-volatility (extreme variance). The HMM filter produces real-time posterior state probability estimates that can be read as continuous regime indicators. Applied uniformly to 15 futures instruments (4 commodity, 4 currency, 4 equity, 3 fixed income; 4972 daily observations Jan 2000 – Oct 2019). Three states selected via greedy model selection (Nguyen 2021). hmm_filtered_state_probability_bull; hmm_filtered_state_probability_bear; hmm_filtered_state_probability_high_vol; ewmm_return_mean; ewmm_return_variance The asset-independent design is a key feature: the same HMM framework applies to commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income futures without modification. EWMM span parameter controls responsiveness (lower span = faster regime detection but higher turnover; span=30 recommended). Three-state structure identified via greedy approach; alternative state counts were not systematically validated.

The Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio (PESR) scalar signal and associated out-of-sample risk-adjusted return performance across multi-asset futures. PESR is defined as PESR = (ESR)^T * alpha_{n+h|n}, where ESR_j is the state-level expected Sharpe ratio estimated from EWMM features in hidden state j, and alpha_{n+h|n} = alpha_{n|n} * A^h is the h-step-ahead predicted state probability vector computed by multiplying the current filtered state vector by the h-th power of the transition matrix A. PESR is a scalar forward-looking risk-adjusted return predictor; positions are set proportional to its sign and magnitude (long-only: max(0, PESR)). OOS long-only strategy (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019, span=30, 5bps transaction costs) achieves substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold for most of 15 futures instruments: EQ4 SR=3.0 vs. B&H 1.0; FI1 SR=1.91 vs. 0.27; CO1 SR=2.4 vs. 0.67 (Nguyen 2021, Tables 3-4). pesr_scalar_signal; hmm_predicted_state_probability_h_step; state_level_expected_sharpe_ratio; oos_sharpe_ratio; buy_and_hold_sharpe_ratio PESR is both the decision rule (translating regime probabilities into positions) and the performance signal (higher OOS SR when PESR accurately predicts regimes). OOS test period is relatively short (approximately 4 years, Jan 2016–Oct 2019). Source is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. The combination of preprint source and short OOS window warrants some evidence discount, though the magnitude of SR improvement across multiple asset classes is striking.

In out-of-sample testing (January 2016 – October 2019), the HMM long-only strategy with EWMM span=30 achieves Sharpe ratios substantially above buy-and-hold for most instruments at 5bps transaction costs: EQ4 achieves SR=3.0 vs buy-and-hold SR=1.0, FI1 achieves SR=1.91 vs SR=0.27, and CO1 achieves SR=2.4 vs SR=0.67. Overall, span=30 produces SR>1 for most of the 15 instruments. Tables 3 and 4, p.5-6. Test period: Jan 2016 – Oct 2019 (approximately 4 years). Training: through 2012; validation: 2012-2016. Strategy is long- only with holdings capped at [0,1]. 5bps transaction cost per trade applied.

The Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio (PESR) metric is defined as PESR^S_i(h) = (ESR^S)^T * alpha_{n+h|n}, where ESR^S_j = mu_j(f_s^1) / mu_j(f_s^2) is the expected Sharpe ratio in hidden state j estimated from EWMM features, and alpha_{n+h|n} = alpha_{n|n} * A^h is the h-step-ahead state probability vector computed from the transition matrix. This scalar metric predicts risk-adjusted returns h steps ahead. Section 4.3 and Equation (4.1), p.4. The metric translates regime probabilities into a forward-looking SR forecast by combining state-level SR estimates with HMM-predicted state probabilities. Portfolio positions are set proportional to PESR sign and magnitude.

The EWMM span parameter s controls regime stickiness: lower s makes features more responsive to recent data, increasing regime transition frequency and portfolio turnover; higher s smooths features more heavily, reducing turnover but slowing regime detection. Span s=30 corresponds to approximately 25-60 day rebalancing intervals and provides a favorable tradeoff between SR performance and transaction costs across most instruments. Sections 4.2 and 5, p.4-6. Spans s in {15, 30, 60} tested. Lower s increases the number of regime changes and thus turnover (daily turnover ranges roughly from 1.64% to 4.87% for s=15 vs. 2.54% for s=30 for some instruments). Higher s reduces responsiveness and may miss genuine regime shifts.

A three-state hidden Markov model applied asset-independently to daily futures returns on 15 instruments across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income classes identifies three regimes labeled bull, bear, and high-volatility. The model uses EWMM features of first and second moments (mean and variance of returns) as the observation vector, normalized and concatenated for each instrument independently. Abstract and Sections 1, 2.1, 3, p.1-3. Data: 4972 daily closing return observations per instrument, January 2000 – October 2019. Three states chosen via greedy approach. The asset-independent design applies the same HMM framework to any asset class without modification.

regime_switch Use EWMM features (first and second moments of daily returns with span=30) as inputs to a three-state HMM for real-time regime identification across multi- asset futures. The normalized EWMM observation vector is applicable across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income asset classes without modification, enabling a consistent cross-asset regime identification framework. HMM-filtered state probabilities (bull, bear, high-volatility) serve as the primary regime features for downstream position sizing and risk control. The three-state HMM (bull/bear/high-volatility) trained per instrument provides the regime state probability estimates used as model inputs. The PESR decision rule (PESR = ESR^T * alpha_{n+h|n}) translates h-step-ahead predicted regime probabilities into a scalar risk-adjusted return forecast. OOS evidence supports substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold for most of 15 futures instruments at 5bps transaction costs (Jan 2016–Oct 2019). Three-state structure selected via greedy approach; alternative state counts require validation before use in production. Confidence in HMM regime signal quality should be conditioned on EWMM span calibration: span=30 provides a favorable SR/turnover tradeoff in the OOS test period. High-confidence long positions are indicated when PESR is substantially positive; positions should be exited or reduced when PESR approaches zero or turns negative. Source is a preprint; confidence in robustness of OOS results requires corroboration from additional validation periods and asset classes. Suppress activity when HMM assigns high posterior probability to the high-volatility state (bear or high-vol dominant); reduce or close long positions when the predicted regime over the h-step horizon is unfavorable. OOS test period is approximately 4 years (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019); short window may not adequately capture multiple full market cycles. Results are from a preprint, not peer-reviewed. Long-only strategy design limits applicability to directional long strategies; extension to long/short requires separate validation. Transaction cost sensitivity should be tested at costs above 5bps.

position_sizing Use the PESR scalar metric as the primary position-sizing signal for multi-asset futures strategies. PESR = (ESR)^T * alpha_{n+h|n} combines state-level Sharpe estimates with h-step-ahead predicted regime probabilities, providing a forward- looking risk-adjusted return forecast per instrument. EWMM span=30 is recommended as the baseline calibration for the EWMM features feeding the HMM (approximately 25-60 day rebalancing intervals, daily turnover ~2.54% for representative instruments in the OOS test period). Calibrate span on a validation period before production deployment. Position sizes in a long-only strategy should be set proportional to max(0, PESR); instruments with PESR>0 receive positive allocations, PESR<=0 instruments receive zero (no position). The h-step-ahead transition matrix power (A^h) determines forecast horizon; select h based on expected holding period and rebalancing frequency. The EWMM span controls the sensitivity/smoothness tradeoff: lower span increases position turnover; higher span increases detection lag. At 5bps transaction costs with span=30, OOS SR substantially exceeds buy-and-hold for most of 15 instruments (EQ4: 3.0 vs. 1.0; FI1: 1.91 vs. 0.27; CO1: 2.4 vs. 0.67). PESR magnitude provides a natural confidence signal: large positive PESR indicates high confidence in the bull state; PESR near zero indicates low confidence or regime uncertainty. Position size proportional to PESR magnitude implements implicit confidence-weighted scaling. Reduce positions when PESR is small in magnitude, reflecting mixed or uncertain regime signals. Zero positions when PESR<=0 (long-only mode). Consider reducing all position sizes proportionally when HMM assigns high posterior probability to the high-volatility state across multiple instruments simultaneously, as this may indicate a broad market stress episode. The PESR position sizing rule is definitional (evidence_tier=3); empirical performance evidence is in claim_nguyen_oos_sharpe_003. Span tradeoff evidence (evidence_tier=2) calibrates the key hyperparameter. Both the span calibration and OOS results are from a preprint on a short test window; the position sizing rule is well-designed but production deployment warrants additional validation on longer periods and real-time transaction cost estimates.

The three-state HMM structure (bull, bear, high-volatility) was selected via a greedy model selection procedure applied uniformly across all 15 futures instruments. Greedy selection does not guarantee globally optimal state count and may produce suboptimal regime identification for instruments whose return dynamics are better described by a different number of states. For some instruments, a two-state model (bull/bear only) or a four-state model (with an additional low-volatility or trend-reversal state) may better capture the empirical return distribution. The uniform application of a single three-state architecture across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income futures ignores the possibility that different asset classes exhibit structurally different regime counts. Additionally, the same three-state labels (bull, bear, high-volatility) applied to all instruments may not have consistent economic interpretation across asset classes: a "bull" state in commodity futures differs materially from a "bull" state in fixed income futures. Misspecified state counts produce regime filter outputs that conflate distinct market conditions into merged states or split single conditions into spurious sub-states. When the three-state structure does not adequately capture the return dynamics of a specific instrument or asset class; when applying the model to instruments outside the training set of 15 futures contracts; when economic interpretation of state labels is required to be consistent across asset classes. The greedy selection procedure was not cross-validated on held-out instruments or time periods. The preprint does not report systematic model selection criteria (e.g., BIC, AIC, likelihood ratio tests) across different state counts to justify the three-state choice. Sensitivity analysis with two- and four-state variants would materially strengthen confidence in the three-state specification.

The out-of-sample test window used to validate the HMM long-only strategy (January 2016 – October 2019, approximately 4 years) is short and covers a predominantly bull-market phase for equities and a generally favorable period for trend-following in multiple asset classes.
