[state] Long-Horizon Equity Mean Reversion State. A market condition in which equity returns exhibit positive serial correlation at horizons shorter than one year and negative serial correlation (mean reversion) at longer horizons of 3–8 years, implying a large transitory mean-reverting price component. Characterized by: (1) positive autocorrelation at monthly and sub-annual horizons flipping to negative at 3–8 year horizons in NYSE value-weighted and equal-weighted CRSP indexes (1926–1985); (2) the transitory component's standard deviation estimated at 15–25% for the value-weighted index and up to 37% for the equal-weighted index, accounting for more than 50% of monthly return variance in the equal-weighted case; (3) the pattern confirmed in 15 of 17 international equity markets, with less-developed markets showing stronger mean reversion consistent with greater noise trader activity; (4) a pure risk-based explanation would require time-varying required return volatility of 5–15%+ per year—implausibly large relative to empirical risk premium estimates—ruling out efficient-market risk-premium variation as the primary driver; (5) variance ratio tests have only 6–19% power against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share, so failure to reject the random walk cannot be taken as evidence against long-horizon mean reversion. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988), Journal of Financial Economics, evidence_tier 1.
[signature_poterba_summers_cross_market_confirmation_003] Observable cross-market corroboration of the long-horizon mean reversion state across 17 international equity markets, providing a breadth-based signature that supplements single-market statistical tests limited by low power. The signature is detectable as: (1) count of national equity markets showing negative long-horizon variance ratios (VR(q) < 1 at 3–8 year horizons)—15 of 17 markets confirmed in the Poterba and Summers (1988) international analysis, covering Morgan Stanley Capital International indexes approximately 1957–1985; (2) stronger negative long-horizon autocorrelation in less-developed or less liquid markets relative to developed markets, consistent with greater noise trader activity and lower speed of arbitrage; (3) directional consistency of the sign-flip pattern across markets (positive sub-annual, negative multi-year) even when individual-market test statistics do not achieve conventional significance levels; (4) standardized cross-market vote count (number of markets with VR(q) < 1 at 3–5 year horizons) as a pooled confidence indicator. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988), Section IV. international_market_count_vr_negative; international_market_vr_5yr_sign; emerging_vs_developed_vr_differential; pooled_cross_market_vr_statistic; noise_trader_activity_proxy The 15/17 cross-market hit rate is the primary evidence for the robustness of the long-horizon mean reversion state, given that individual-market power is only 6–19%. The signature is qualitatively robust (direction of effect) even if quantitatively imprecise (magnitude varies by market). The finding that less-developed markets show stronger mean reversion is consistent with the noise trader hypothesis (DeLong, Shleifer, Summers, and Waldmann 1990): markets with less sophisticated investors and less effective arbitrage sustain larger transitory deviations. This cross-market signature is a validation tool for the state primitive, not a trading signal.
[signature_poterba_summers_horizon_autocorr_flip_001] Observable sign reversal in equity return serial correlation as the measurement horizon extends from sub-annual to multi-year, providing the primary empirical signature of the long-horizon mean reversion state. The signature is measurable as: (1) positive serial correlation at return horizons shorter than one year (monthly autocorrelations positive); (2) negative serial correlation (variance ratio VR(q) < 1) at return horizons of 3–8 years; (3) the sign-flip pattern confirmed in 15 of 17 international equity markets (Morgan Stanley Capital International data, approximately 1957–1985), with less-developed markets showing stronger negative long-horizon autocorrelation; (4) the most negative variance ratios appearing in the 3–5 year return window in U.S. data. Computed on NYSE value-weighted and equal-weighted CRSP indexes (1926–1985) using monthly, annual, and multi-year overlapping return windows. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988), Journal of Financial Economics, evidence_tier 1. variance_ratio_monthly; variance_ratio_annual; variance_ratio_3yr; variance_ratio_5yr; variance_ratio_8yr; autocorrelation_long_horizon; international_market_vr_sign The sign-flip is the central empirical fact: positive autocorrelation at sub-annual horizons (consistent with Lo-MacKinlay's weekly findings) transitions to negative autocorrelation at multi-year horizons. The 15/17 international hit rate provides breadth of confirmation but individual-market statistical power is low (6–19%; see claim_poterba_summers_test_power_004). Less-developed markets showing stronger mean reversion connects to noise trader models where higher noise trading activity creates a more pronounced transitory price component.
[signature_poterba_summers_power_calibration_004] Observable power-calibration signal for long-horizon variance ratio tests, quantifying the likelihood that a non-rejection of the random walk reflects true absence of mean reversion versus insufficient statistical power. The signature is computable as: (1) the Poterba-Summers Monte Carlo power estimates against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share: 6% power (shorter samples, approximately 20–30 years) to 19% power (longer samples, approximately 60 years)—implying that a non-rejection of the random walk is expected in 81–94% of tests even when mean reversion is genuinely present; (2) sample length as a power indicator—each additional decade of data increases power toward the 19% upper bound (at 60+ years of data), but power never reaches conventional adequacy (e.g., 80%) with available sample lengths; (3) the ratio of cross-market confirmations (15/17 ≈ 88%) relative to the expected number under the null of no mean reversion (approximately 50% by chance) as a power-adjusted joint test—the 15/17 outcome is highly unlikely under the no-mean-reversion null; (4) power-adjusted p-value for individual-market tests using the 6–19% power range as a correction factor for interpreting conventional test results. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988) Monte Carlo simulations. sample_length_years; estimated_test_power_percent; cross_market_vr_negative_count; expected_count_under_null; power_adjusted_inference_flag; transitory_half_life_estimate The 6–19% power range is the key calibration for interpreting long-horizon variance ratio test results. A test with 6% power against a specific alternative is essentially non-informative for that alternative; the 19% upper bound at maximal sample length is still well below the 80% power typically required for reliable inference. This signature quantifies the inferential limitation rather than the economic phenomenon itself. It is a methodological quality indicator that should accompany any interpretation of long-horizon mean reversion test results.
[signature_poterba_summers_transitory_variance_002] Observable magnitude of the transitory (mean-reverting) component of equity prices as estimated through variance ratio decomposition, quantifying the economic significance of the long-horizon mean reversion state. The signature is measurable as: (1) standard deviation of the transitory component estimated at 15–25% for the NYSE value-weighted index (1926–1985); (2) up to 37% for the equal-weighted NYSE index; (3) the transitory component accounting for more than 50% of total monthly return variance in the equal-weighted case; (4) the AR(1) approximation to the mean-reversion process implies a half-life of approximately 2.9 years for the transitory component. The 37% transitory volatility for the equal-weighted index implies that roughly half of all short-horizon equity price moves have no permanent information content and will ultimately be reversed. Estimated via variance ratio decomposition and AR(1) approximation, NYSE CRSP data 1926–1985. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988) Tables 1–3. transitory_component_stddev_vw; transitory_component_stddev_ew; transitory_variance_share_monthly; mean_reversion_half_life_years; permanent_component_stddev; variance_ratio_decomposition The 15–25% (value-weighted) and up to 37% (equal-weighted) transitory volatility estimates are derived from variance ratio profiles via an AR(1) mean-reversion approximation, not direct measurement. The equal- weighted index shows larger transitory component, consistent with the Lo-MacKinlay finding of stronger autocorrelation in smaller-cap stocks. The 2.9-year half-life and 75% transitory variance share are the benchmark parameters used in Poterba-Summers power calculations showing only 6–19% test power (claim_poterba_summers_test_power_004).
[claim_poterba_summers_horizon_pattern_001] U.S. equity returns exhibit positive serial correlation at horizons shorter than one year and negative serial correlation (mean reversion) at longer horizons of 3 to 8 years. This horizon-dependent autocorrelation structure implies that stock prices contain a transitory component that generates short-term positive momentum followed by long-term mean reversion. Poterba and Summers (1988) analyze the NYSE value-weighted and equal-weighted indexes over 1926–1985 using both autocorrelation tests and variance ratio tests. Section II presents autocorrelation estimates at monthly through multi-year horizons. The sign pattern (positive at short horizons, negative at long horizons) is the paper's central empirical claim, distinguished from the random walk and from pure mean reversion.
[claim_poterba_summers_international_003] Long-horizon mean reversion in equity returns is confirmed in 15 of 17 international equity markets studied. Markets with less sophisticated investor bases or less liquid trading conditions show stronger mean reversion than developed markets, consistent with the hypothesis that noise trading is more prevalent in those markets. Section IV of Poterba and Summers (1988) extends the variance ratio analysis to 18 national equity markets (17 international + U.S.). The systematic sign of negative long-horizon serial correlation in 15 of 17 markets provides out-of-sample confirmation of the U.S. result. The authors note that emerging and less liquid markets tend to show larger negative variance ratios at long horizons, which they interpret as evidence for noise trader activity.
[claim_poterba_summers_risk_explanation_005] A risk-based explanation of long-horizon mean reversion would require the standard deviation of time-varying required returns to be 5–15% or more per year, depending on the assumed mean-reversion speed. This level of required return variability is implausibly large given typical estimates of risk premium variation, making pure risk-factor explanations insufficient to account for the observed mean reversion pattern. Section VI of Poterba and Summers (1988) evaluates whether time-varying required returns (risk premiums) could generate the observed variance ratio pattern without implying market inefficiency. Using the transitory component model as a benchmark, they calculate the required volatility of discount rate changes needed to produce the observed negative long-horizon serial correlation. The implied discount rate volatility (5–15%+ per year) far exceeds empirical estimates of equity risk premium variation from consumption-based models or dividend-yield models.
[claim_poterba_summers_test_power_004] Variance ratio tests, while the most powerful available tests for detecting long-horizon mean reversion, have severely limited statistical power against economically plausible alternatives. Against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life of 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share, the variance ratio test has only 6–19% power at the 5% significance level, depending on sample length. A century of data would typically yield fewer than one statistically significant rejection. Section V of Poterba and Summers (1988) conducts Monte Carlo simulations to assess the power of variance ratio and related tests under the alternative hypothesis of the plausible transitory component model estimated from U.S. data. The simulation generates artificial samples matching the estimated parameters (half-life 2.9 years, 75% transitory share) and applies the same tests. Power at 5% size is 6% for the shortest samples and up to 19% for longer historical windows — meaning the test fails to reject the null 80–94% of the time even when the alternative is true.
[claim_poterba_summers_transitory_magnitude_002] The estimated standard deviation of the transitory (mean-reverting) component of stock prices is 15–25% for the NYSE value-weighted index and up to 37% for the equal-weighted index. This transitory component accounts for more than 50% of total monthly return variance in the equal-weighted case, implying that the majority of short-horizon equity price movements are ultimately reversed. Tables 1–3 and Section III of Poterba and Summers (1988) estimate the magnitude of the transitory component using a decomposition of stock prices into permanent (random walk) and transitory (mean-reverting) components. The 15–25% (value-weighted) and up to 37% (equal-weighted) figures refer to the standard deviation of the transitory component as a percentage of stock price. The >50% monthly variance share (equal-weighted) is derived from the variance ratio estimates.
[policy_poterba_summers_horizon_regime_switch_001] regime_switch The sign reversal in equity return autocorrelation from positive (sub-annual) to negative (3–8 year) requires a horizon-conditional regime-switch policy that selects the appropriate predictability mechanism based on the measurement horizon. Features for horizon-conditioned regime switching: (1) return horizon indicator—a categorical feature identifying whether the current analysis targets sub-annual (Lo-MacKinlay positive autocorrelation regime) or multi-year (Poterba-Summers negative autocorrelation / mean reversion regime); (2) variance ratio sign—VR(q) > 1 at short horizons (q ≤ 4 quarters) signals the momentum regime; VR(q) < 1 at long horizons (q = 3–8 years) signals the mean reversion regime; (3) rolling variance ratio computed at multiple horizons simultaneously to monitor horizon-conditional regime state; (4) current-period alignment with the sign-flip pattern—confirming that positive autocorrelation persists at sub-annual horizons while negative autocorrelation is present at 3–5 year horizons, consistent with the 1926–1985 pattern. Switch model signals between the short-horizon momentum framework (positive autocorrelation at sub-annual horizons, from Lo-MacKinlay) and the long-horizon contrarian framework (negative autocorrelation at 3–8 year horizons, from Poterba-Summers) based on the measurement horizon. These two states are empirically compatible and can coexist in the same market: short-term momentum and long-term mean reversion represent different time scales of the same price adjustment process. Do not apply short-horizon momentum signals at multi-year horizons, or long-horizon contrarian signals at weekly horizons. Confidence in the horizon-flipping pattern is highest for: (1) equity index data (not individual stocks) where the index-level autocorrelation is strongest; (2) equal-weighted or value-weighted NYSE indexes which were the primary evidence base in Poterba-Summers (1926–1985); (3) multi-market corroboration (15/17 international markets showing the same pattern). Single-market single-period tests have low power (6–19%) to confirm the sign flip; absence of statistical rejection at long horizons should not reduce regime-switch confidence. The Poterba-Summers long-horizon mean reversion state and the Lo-MacKinlay short-horizon predictability state are complementary, not contradictory. They operate at different time scales and have different economic mechanisms. The horizon-conditional regime switch is the appropriate policy response, not a choice between the two states. The 3–8 year mean reversion horizon implies that any practical long-horizon contrarian strategy requires multi-year holding periods, limiting its utility for shorter-horizon trading frameworks.
[policy_poterba_summers_long_horizon_001] confidence_calibration When the long-horizon mean reversion state is classified as active, emphasize: (1) long-horizon variance ratio features at 3–8 year windows as primary state indicators (sign flip from positive to negative signals mean reversion regime); (2) transitory component magnitude proxies—long-horizon return reversal indicators calibrated to the 15–25% (value-weighted) and up to 37% (equal-weighted) transitory standard deviation estimates; (3) international cross-market confirmation features: number of markets showing negative long-horizon VR out of a panel (15/17 benchmark); (4) noise-trading or sentiment proxy features consistent with the behavioral explanation of the transitory component. De-emphasize short-horizon momentum features that apply to the positive sub-annual autocorrelation, which is a different regime from the 3–8 year mean reversion state. Long-horizon contrarian strategies (long multi-year underperformers, short multi-year outperformers) should be calibrated using the transitory component parameters: half-life ≈ 2.9 years, transitory volatility 15–37%. The horizon where mean reversion is strongest is 3–5 years for U.S. data. International corroboration (15/17 markets) supports treating this as a robust cross-market state. Risk-based explanations are insufficient at empirically calibrated magnitudes (see failure_poterba_summers_risk_explanation_005), pointing toward behavioral/noise-trading models as the preferred mechanism. Calibrate confidence in the long-horizon mean reversion state using the cross-market count (15/17) as the primary evidence, not individual-market test statistics. Individual-market variance ratio tests have only 6–19% power (see failure_poterba_summers_test_power_004); absence of rejection in a single market should not reduce confidence in the state. The transitory component magnitude (15–37%) provides an upper bound on economically achievable returns from long-horizon contrarian strategies. Suppress long-horizon contrarian activity when the trading horizon is shorter than 3 years (the state is defined at 3–8 year horizons; shorter horizons exhibit the complementary positive autocorrelation state). Also suppress when available sample evidence (current market) does not corroborate the horizon sign-flip pattern. The reduced_activity mode reflects the long-horizon nature of the state: it requires multi-year holding periods and has limited high-frequency signal value. The 50%+ monthly variance attributable to the transitory component in the equal-weighted case is a striking estimate that justifies long-horizon contrarian positions, but the low test power (6–19%) means this magnitude cannot be verified with high statistical confidence from typical sample sizes.
[policy_poterba_summers_risk_model_selection_005] model_weighting The Poterba-Summers calibration showing that a pure time-varying risk premium explanation requires 5–15%+ annual required return volatility—exceeding standard empirical risk premium estimates—implies that risk-based and behavioral models should receive differential weighting when explaining or trading the long-horizon mean reversion state. Features for model selection: (1) empirical risk premium volatility estimate from available data (dividend yields, consumption-based models, survey expectations)—if below 5% annually, risk-based models are unlikely to account for the full transitory component magnitude; (2) the implied discount rate volatility required by any proposed risk-based model to match the 15–25% (VW) or 37% (EW) transitory standard deviation—models requiring >15% discount rate volatility per year should be flagged as quantitatively implausible under standard asset pricing frameworks; (3) post-1988 risk model developments (e.g., Campbell-Cochrane 1999 habit formation) as a feature indicating whether the risk-based explanation has been strengthened by subsequent work. When modeling the long-horizon mean reversion state, assign higher weight to behavioral (noise-trading) mechanisms than to time-varying rational risk premium mechanisms at Poterba-Summers calibrations, unless the proposed risk model can generate ≥ 5% annual required return volatility under empirically supported parameter assumptions. The Campbell-Cochrane (1999) caveat applies: habit formation models can generate larger risk premium variation and may partially restore the rational explanation, but this evidence was not available in the original Poterba-Summers analysis and should be incorporated as an update to the prior. Model weighting should reflect the empirical evidence available at the time of application. Confidence that the long-horizon mean reversion state reflects genuine excess price movements (beyond rational risk compensation) is high given the implausibility of the required 5–15% risk premium volatility in standard models. This does not rule out all rational explanations; it reduces confidence in the specific channel of time-varying required returns as the primary driver. Uncertainty about the mechanism (behavioral vs. risk-based) should be reflected as model uncertainty, not as uncertainty about the empirical mean reversion pattern itself, which is well-documented across markets and time periods. The 5–15% required return volatility benchmark is a calibration result conditional on the AR(1) mean-reversion model parameters estimated from the 1926–1985 data. Subsequent habit formation models (Campbell-Cochrane 1999) generate large risk premium variation through slow-moving internal habit, potentially reconciling rational pricing with the observed mean reversion. The Poterba-Summers analysis predates this literature; the policy implication applies specifically to simpler rational expectation models that were the relevant alternatives in 1988.
[policy_poterba_summers_test_power_004] confidence_calibration When evaluating evidence for or against the long-horizon mean reversion state, adjust inference for the known 6–19% power of variance ratio tests against the empirically calibrated mean-reversion alternative. Key features for power-adjusted inference: (1) sample length indicator—for samples shorter than 60 years, power falls toward the 6% lower bound, making non-rejection uninformative; (2) international panel count—use the number of markets showing the pattern (15/17 benchmark) rather than individual-market test statistics as the primary evidence feature; (3) implied discount rate volatility from any proposed risk-premium explanation—flag explanations requiring >5–15% annual required-return volatility as inconsistent with empirical risk premium estimates; (4) power simulation results conditional on estimated half-life (2.9 years) and transitory variance share (75%). Do not use p-values from individual-market long-horizon variance ratio tests as the primary evidence for or against the mean reversion state. A p-value above 0.05 in a single-market test with 60 years of data is expected under the mean-reversion alternative 80–94% of the time. Construct model evidence using pooled cross-market evidence (15/17 markets) and economically calibrated prior beliefs about transitory component magnitude, not frequentist rejection rates from low-power tests. Treat the following inference correctly: non-rejection of the random walk in a single long-horizon test is weak evidence against mean reversion given 6–19% power. Non-rejection cannot be symmetric with rejection in this context. Confidence in the mean reversion state should remain material unless rejected across multiple long-horizon sample periods and multiple markets with corroborating evidence. Likewise, a pure risk-based explanation that requires 5–15%+ discount rate volatility should reduce confidence in that mechanism, not in the empirical mean-reversion pattern itself. The power-adjusted inference policy is a methodological correction for all long-horizon predictability research, not just the mean reversion state. It applies whenever variance ratio tests or related tests are used to assess 3–8 year return predictability. The practical implication for market state classification is that "state inactive" declarations for the long-horizon mean reversion state require strong positive evidence, not merely absence of statistically significant variance ratio test rejections.
[policy_poterba_summers_transitory_position_sizing_002] position_sizing The transitory component magnitude—standard deviation 15–25% for the NYSE value-weighted index and up to 37% for the equal-weighted index (1926–1985), with a half-life of approximately 2.9 years—establishes the economically achievable return bounds for long-horizon contrarian strategies. Scale long-horizon contrarian position sizes to the estimated transitory component magnitude. The 37% equal-weighted and 15–25% value-weighted transitory standard deviations set the upper bounds on expected mean-reversion return over a full half-life (2.9 years). Positions should not assume immediate reversion; the 2.9-year half-life means that in any given year, only a fraction of the outstanding transitory deviation will revert on average. Do not size positions based on the full transitory component magnitude as if immediate full reversion were expected; apply a fraction consistent with the expected partial reversion over the intended holding horizon. Confidence in transitory component magnitude estimates (15–25% VW, 37% EW) is calibrated to the full 1926–1985 sample period; the estimates are derived from variance ratio decomposition, not direct measurement. The 6–19% test power caveat applies: the transitory component magnitude cannot be precisely estimated from a single market's sample, and cross-market confirmation (15/17 markets showing the pattern) is the primary evidence for its existence. Position size confidence should be scaled down proportionally with the statistical uncertainty in the transitory component estimate. Suppress long-horizon contrarian positions when the intended holding period is less than the 2.9-year half-life, as the expected fraction of transitory component reversion is insufficient to generate material expected returns within the holding period. Also suppress when current-period equal-weighted or value-weighted index returns are not consistent with the sign-flip pattern (i.e., when short-horizon and long-horizon autocorrelations have the same sign). The 15–25% (VW) and 37% (EW) transitory standard deviation estimates are the parameter inputs for scaling long-horizon contrarian positions; they represent the economically available mean-reversion opportunity, not the risk of the position. The half-life of 2.9 years and the 75% transitory variance share (used in power calculations) are AR(1) approximation parameters. These figures should be treated as calibration benchmarks from the historical sample and verified against more recent data before operational use.
[failure_poterba_summers_risk_explanation_005] Models that attribute the long-horizon mean reversion state entirely to time-varying rational risk premiums (efficient markets interpretation) require implausibly large discount rate volatility to match the observed transitory component magnitude. Poterba and Summers (1988) calibrate that generating the observed negative long-horizon serial correlation through time-varying required returns alone would require the standard deviation of annual required return changes to be 5–15% or more, depending on the assumed mean-reversion speed. This level of required return variability far exceeds empirical estimates of equity risk premium variation from consumption-based models, dividend-yield regressions, or other standard asset pricing frameworks available in 1988. A model that treats the long-horizon mean reversion state as fully compatible with rational risk-premium variation, without verifying that the required risk premium volatility falls within empirically plausible bounds, will misclassify a behaviorally-driven price pattern as a risk-compensated regime. The practical failure is treating the mean-reversion state as tradeable on risk-premium grounds when the identified channel requires implausible parameter magnitudes. When time-varying risk premium models are applied to the long-horizon mean reversion state without checking whether the implied discount rate volatility (5–15%+ per year) is consistent with empirical risk premium estimates; when habit formation or other non-standard consumption models that can generate larger risk premium variation (e.g., Campbell-Cochrane 1999) are unavailable or not applied; when the noise-trading or behavioral explanation is rejected solely on theoretical grounds without calibrating the risk-based alternative's quantitative requirements. Subsequent work challenges Poterba-Summers on this point: Campbell and Cochrane (1999) habit formation generates risk premium variation large enough to partially explain long-horizon mean reversion without noise trading. The risk-based explanation has not been definitively ruled out by later literature. The 5–15% required return volatility threshold remains a useful calibration benchmark for evaluating whether a proposed risk factor can account for the observed transitory component magnitude.
[failure_poterba_summers_test_power_004] Long-horizon variance ratio tests and related statistical procedures have severely limited power to detect the long-horizon mean reversion state even when it is present and economically significant. Monte Carlo simulations by Poterba and Summers (1988) show that against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share—parameters estimated from the U.S. data—variance ratio tests have power of only 6–19% at the 5% significance level, depending on sample length. This means the test fails to reject the random walk null 80–94% of the time even when the long-horizon mean reversion state is genuinely active. Failure to achieve statistical rejection of the random walk at long horizons cannot be interpreted as absence of mean reversion; such non-rejections are expected under the mean-reversion alternative. Any model that uses p-value thresholds to decide whether the long-horizon mean reversion state is "active" will frequently classify the state as inactive when it is in fact present, generating systematic false negatives. When absence of statistically significant rejection of the random walk at 3–8 year horizons is treated as evidence that the long-horizon mean reversion state is inactive; when the 6–19% power calculation is not applied to calibrate expected false-negative rates; when sample periods shorter than 60 years are used to test long-horizon mean reversion with the expectation of obtaining reliable power; when pooled international evidence is not used to compensate for the low individual-market power. The 6% lower bound (shortest samples) to 19% upper bound (longer samples) implies that even with 60+ years of data, the probability of correctly detecting mean reversion in a single market using variance ratio tests is below one in five. The cross-market analysis (15/17 markets showing the pattern) is the primary evidence precisely because individual-market tests lack power; pooling provides a joint signal where individual tests cannot. This is a fundamental methodological caveat for all long-horizon predictability studies.

Features for horizon-conditioned regime switching: (1) return horizon indicator—a categorical feature identifying whether the current analysis targets sub-annual (Lo-MacKinlay positive autocorrelation regime) or multi-year (Poterba-Summers negative autocorrelation / mean reversion regime); (2) variance ratio sign—VR(q) > 1 at short horizons (q ≤ 4 quarters) signals the momentum regime; VR(q) < 1 at long horizons (q = 3–8 years) signals the mean reversion regime; (3) rolling variance ratio computed at multiple horizons simultaneously to monitor horizon-conditional regime state; (4) current-period alignment with the sign-flip pattern—confirming that positive autocorrelation persists at sub-annual horizons while negative autocorrelation is present at 3–5 year horizons, consistent with the 1926–1985 pattern. Switch model signals between the short-horizon momentum framework (positive autocorrelation at sub-annual horizons, from Lo-MacKinlay) and the long-horizon contrarian framework (negative autocorrelation at 3–8 year horizons, from Poterba-Summers) based on the measurement horizon. These two states are empirically compatible and can coexist in the same market: short-term momentum and long-term mean reversion represent different time scales of the same price adjustment process. Do not apply short-horizon momentum signals at multi-year horizons, or long-horizon contrarian signals at weekly horizons. Confidence in the horizon-flipping pattern is highest for: (1) equity index data (not individual stocks) where the index-level autocorrelation is strongest; (2) equal-weighted or value-weighted NYSE indexes which were the primary evidence base in Poterba-Summers (1926–1985); (3) multi-market corroboration (15/17 international markets showing the same pattern). Single-market single-period tests have low power (6–19%) to confirm the sign flip; absence of statistical rejection at long horizons should not reduce regime-switch confidence. The Poterba-Summers long-horizon mean reversion state and the Lo-MacKinlay short-horizon predictability state are complementary, not contradictory. They operate at different time scales and have different economic mechanisms. The horizon-conditional regime switch is the appropriate policy response, not a choice between the two states. The 3–8 year mean reversion horizon implies that any practical long-horizon contrarian strategy requires multi-year holding periods, limiting its utility for shorter-horizon trading frameworks.

confidence_calibration When the long-horizon mean reversion state is classified as active, emphasize: (1) long-horizon variance ratio features at 3–8 year windows as primary state indicators (sign flip from positive to negative signals mean reversion regime); (2) transitory component magnitude proxies—long-horizon return reversal indicators calibrated to the 15–25% (value-weighted) and up to 37% (equal-weighted) transitory standard deviation estimates; (3) international cross-market confirmation features: number of markets showing negative long-horizon VR out of a panel (15/17 benchmark); (4) noise-trading or sentiment proxy features consistent with the behavioral explanation of the transitory component. De-emphasize short-horizon momentum features that apply to the positive sub-annual autocorrelation, which is a different regime from the 3–8 year mean reversion state. Long-horizon contrarian strategies (long multi-year underperformers, short multi-year outperformers) should be calibrated using the transitory component parameters: half-life ≈ 2.9 years, transitory volatility 15–37%. The horizon where mean reversion is strongest is 3–5 years for U.S. data. International corroboration (15/17 markets) supports treating this as a robust cross-market state. Risk-based explanations are insufficient at empirically calibrated magnitudes (see failure_poterba_summers_risk_explanation_005), pointing toward behavioral/noise-trading models as the preferred mechanism. Calibrate confidence in the long-horizon mean reversion state using the cross-market count (15/17) as the primary evidence, not individual-market test statistics. Individual-market variance ratio tests have only 6–19% power (see failure_poterba_summers_test_power_004); absence of rejection in a single market should not reduce confidence in the state. The transitory component magnitude (15–37%) provides an upper bound on economically achievable returns from long-horizon contrarian strategies. Suppress long-horizon contrarian activity when the trading horizon is shorter than 3 years (the state is defined at 3–8 year horizons; shorter horizons exhibit the complementary positive autocorrelation state). Also suppress when available sample evidence (current market) does not corroborate the horizon sign-flip pattern. The reduced_activity mode reflects the long-horizon nature of the state: it requires multi-year holding periods and has limited high-frequency signal value. The 50%+ monthly variance attributable to the transitory component in the equal-weighted case is a striking estimate that justifies long-horizon contrarian positions, but the low test power (6–19%) means this magnitude cannot be verified with high statistical confidence from typical sample sizes.

model_weighting The Poterba-Summers calibration showing that a pure time-varying risk premium explanation requires 5–15%+ annual required return volatility—exceeding standard empirical risk premium estimates—implies that risk-based and behavioral models should receive differential weighting when explaining or trading the long-horizon mean reversion state. Features for model selection: (1) empirical risk premium volatility estimate from available data (dividend yields, consumption-based models, survey expectations)—if below 5% annually, risk-based models are unlikely to account for the full transitory component magnitude; (2) the implied discount rate volatility required by any proposed risk-based model to match the 15–25% (VW) or 37% (EW) transitory standard deviation—models requiring >15% discount rate volatility per year should be flagged as quantitatively implausible under standard asset pricing frameworks; (3) post-1988 risk model developments (e.g., Campbell-Cochrane 1999 habit formation) as a feature indicating whether the risk-based explanation has been strengthened by subsequent work. When modeling the long-horizon mean reversion state, assign higher weight to behavioral (noise-trading) mechanisms than to time-varying rational risk premium mechanisms at Poterba-Summers calibrations, unless the proposed risk model can generate ≥ 5% annual required return volatility under empirically supported parameter assumptions. The Campbell-Cochrane (1999) caveat applies: habit formation models can generate larger risk premium variation and may partially restore the rational explanation, but this evidence was not available in the original Poterba-Summers analysis and should be incorporated as an update to the prior. Model weighting should reflect the empirical evidence available at the time of application. Confidence that the long-horizon mean reversion state reflects genuine excess price movements (beyond rational risk compensation) is high given the implausibility of the required 5–15% risk premium volatility in standard models. This does not rule out all rational explanations; it reduces confidence in the specific channel of time-varying required returns as the primary driver. Uncertainty about the mechanism (behavioral vs. risk-based) should be reflected as model uncertainty, not as uncertainty about the empirical mean reversion pattern itself, which is well-documented across markets and time periods. The 5–15% required return volatility benchmark is a calibration result conditional on the AR(1) mean-reversion model parameters estimated from the 1926–1985 data. Subsequent habit formation models (Campbell-Cochrane 1999) generate large risk premium variation through slow-moving internal habit, potentially reconciling rational pricing with the observed mean reversion. The Poterba-Summers analysis predates this literature; the policy implication applies specifically to simpler rational expectation models that were the relevant alternatives in 1988.

confidence_calibration When evaluating evidence for or against the long-horizon mean reversion state, adjust inference for the known 6–19% power of variance ratio tests against the empirically calibrated mean-reversion alternative. Key features for power-adjusted inference: (1) sample length indicator—for samples shorter than 60 years, power falls toward the 6% lower bound, making non-rejection uninformative; (2) international panel count—use the number of markets showing the pattern (15/17 benchmark) rather than individual-market test statistics as the primary evidence feature; (3) implied discount rate volatility from any proposed risk-premium explanation—flag explanations requiring >5–15% annual required-return volatility as inconsistent with empirical risk premium estimates; (4) power simulation results conditional on estimated half-life (2.9 years) and transitory variance share (75%). Do not use p-values from individual-market long-horizon variance ratio tests as the primary evidence for or against the mean reversion state. A p-value above 0.05 in a single-market test with 60 years of data is expected under the mean-reversion alternative 80–94% of the time. Construct model evidence using pooled cross-market evidence (15/17 markets) and economically calibrated prior beliefs about transitory component magnitude, not frequentist rejection rates from low-power tests. Treat the following inference correctly: non-rejection of the random walk in a single long-horizon test is weak evidence against mean reversion given 6–19% power. Non-rejection cannot be symmetric with rejection in this context. Confidence in the mean reversion state should remain material unless rejected across multiple long-horizon sample periods and multiple markets with corroborating evidence. Likewise, a pure risk-based explanation that requires 5–15%+ discount rate volatility should reduce confidence in that mechanism, not in the empirical mean-reversion pattern itself. The power-adjusted inference policy is a methodological correction for all long-horizon predictability research, not just the mean reversion state. It applies whenever variance ratio tests or related tests are used to assess 3–8 year return predictability. The practical implication for market state classification is that "state inactive" declarations for the long-horizon mean reversion state require strong positive evidence, not merely absence of statistically significant variance ratio test rejections.

position_sizing The transitory component magnitude—standard deviation 15–25% for the NYSE value-weighted index and up to 37% for the equal-weighted index (1926–1985), with a half-life of approximately 2.9 years—establishes the economically achievable return bounds for long-horizon contrarian strategies. Position sizing features: (1) estimated transitory component standard deviation for the target portfolio (15–25% value-weighted benchmark; up to 37% equal-weighted benchmark) as the maximum potential mean-reversion signal magnitude; (2) the 2.9-year half-life as the minimum holding period for a mean-reversion trade to realize a significant fraction of the transitory component; (3) cumulative multi-year return deviation from trend as a proxy for the current transitory component realization—positions sized proportionally to the estimated outstanding transitory component; (4) value-weighted vs. equal-weighted index type as a feature—equal-weighted portfolios exhibit larger transitory variance, justifying proportionally larger contrarian position sizes for equal-weighted implementations. Scale long-horizon contrarian position sizes to the estimated transitory component magnitude. The 37% equal-weighted and 15–25% value-weighted transitory standard deviations set the upper bounds on expected mean-reversion return over a full half-life (2.9 years). Positions should not assume immediate reversion; the 2.9-year half-life means that in any given year, only a fraction of the outstanding transitory deviation will revert on average. Do not size positions based on the full transitory component magnitude as if immediate full reversion were expected; apply a fraction consistent with the expected partial reversion over the intended holding horizon. Confidence in transitory component magnitude estimates (15–25% VW, 37% EW) is calibrated to the full 1926–1985 sample period; the estimates are derived from variance ratio decomposition, not direct measurement. The 6–19% test power caveat applies: the transitory component magnitude cannot be precisely estimated from a single market's sample, and cross-market confirmation (15/17 markets showing the pattern) is the primary evidence for its existence. Position size confidence should be scaled down proportionally with the statistical uncertainty in the transitory component estimate. Suppress long-horizon contrarian positions when the intended holding period is less than the 2.9-year half-life, as the expected fraction of transitory component reversion is insufficient to generate material expected returns within the holding period. Also suppress when current-period equal-weighted or value-weighted index returns are not consistent with the sign-flip pattern (i.e., when short-horizon and long-horizon autocorrelations have the same sign). The 15–25% (VW) and 37% (EW) transitory standard deviation estimates are the parameter inputs for scaling long-horizon contrarian positions; they represent the economically available mean-reversion opportunity, not the risk of the position. The half-life of 2.9 years and the 75% transitory variance share (used in power calculations) are AR(1) approximation parameters. These figures should be treated as calibration benchmarks from the historical sample and verified against more recent data before operational use.

Models that attribute the long-horizon mean reversion state entirely to time-varying rational risk premiums (efficient markets interpretation) require implausibly large discount rate volatility to match the observed transitory component magnitude. Poterba and Summers (1988) calibrate that generating the observed negative long-horizon serial correlation through time-varying required returns alone would require the standard deviation of annual required return changes to be 5–15% or more, depending on the assumed mean-reversion speed. This level of required return variability far exceeds empirical estimates of equity risk premium variation from consumption-based models, dividend-yield regressions, or other standard asset pricing frameworks available in 1988. A model that treats the long-horizon mean reversion state as fully compatible with rational risk-premium variation, without verifying that the required risk premium volatility falls within empirically plausible bounds, will misclassify a behaviorally-driven price pattern as a risk-compensated regime. The practical failure is treating the mean-reversion state as tradeable on risk-premium grounds when the identified channel requires implausible parameter magnitudes. When time-varying risk premium models are applied to the long-horizon mean reversion state without checking whether the implied discount rate volatility (5–15%+ per year) is consistent with empirical risk premium estimates; when habit formation or other non-standard consumption models that can generate larger risk premium variation (e.g., Campbell-Cochrane 1999) are unavailable or not applied; when the noise-trading or behavioral explanation is rejected solely on theoretical grounds without calibrating the risk-based alternative's quantitative requirements. Subsequent work challenges Poterba-Summers on this point: Campbell and Cochrane (1999) habit formation generates risk premium variation large enough to partially explain long-horizon mean reversion without noise trading. The risk-based explanation has not been definitively ruled out by later literature. The 5–15% required return volatility threshold remains a useful calibration benchmark for evaluating whether a proposed risk factor can account for the observed transitory component magnitude.

Long-horizon variance ratio tests and related statistical procedures have severely limited power to detect the long-horizon mean reversion state even when it is present and economically significant. Monte Carlo simulations by Poterba and Summers (1988) show that against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share—parameters estimated from the U.S. data—variance ratio tests have power of only 6–19% at the 5% significance level, depending on sample length. This means the test fails to reject the random walk null 80–94% of the time even when the long-horizon mean reversion state is genuinely active. Failure to achieve statistical rejection of the random walk at long horizons cannot be interpreted as absence of mean reversion; such non-rejections are expected under the mean-reversion alternative. Any model that uses p-value thresholds to decide whether the long-horizon mean reversion state is "active" will frequently classify the state as inactive when it is in fact present, generating systematic false negatives. When absence of statistically significant rejection of the random walk at 3–8 year horizons is treated as evidence that the long-horizon mean reversion state is inactive; when the 6–19% power calculation is not applied to calibrate expected false-negative rates; when sample periods shorter than 60 years are used to test long-horizon mean reversion with the expectation of obtaining reliable power; when pooled international evidence is not used to compensate for the low individual-market power. The 6% lower bound (shortest samples) to 19% upper bound (longer samples) implies that even with 60+ years of data, the probability of correctly detecting mean reversion in a single market using variance ratio tests is below one in five. The cross-market analysis (15/17 markets showing the pattern) is the primary evidence precisely because individual-market tests lack power; pooling provides a joint signal where individual tests cannot. This is a fundamental methodological caveat for all long-horizon predictability studies.

entries.state_summary: Long-Horizon Equity Mean Reversion State. A market condition in which equity returns exhibit positive serial correlation at horizons shorter than one year and negative serial correlation (mean reversion) at longer horizons of 3–8 years, implying a large transitory mean-reverting price component. Characterized by: (1) positive autocorrelation at monthly and sub-annual horizons flipping to negative at 3–8 year horizons in NYSE value-weighted and equal-weighted CRSP indexes (1926–1985); (2) the transitory component's standard deviation estimated at 15–25% for the value-weighted index and up to 37% for the equal-weighted index, accounting for more than 50% of monthly return variance in the equal-weighted case; (3) the pattern confirmed in 15 of 17 international equity markets, with less-developed markets showing stronger mean reversion consistent with greater noise trader activity; (4) a pure risk-based explanation would require time-varying required return volatility of 5–15%+ per year—implausibly large relative to empirical risk premium estimates—ruling out efficient-market risk-premium variation as the primary driver; (5) variance ratio tests have only 6–19% power against an AR(1) transitory component with half-life 2.9 years and 75% transitory variance share, so failure to reject the random walk cannot be taken as evidence against long-horizon mean reversion. Evidence from Poterba and Summers (1988), Journal of Financial Economics, evidence_tier 1.
